speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we are debating Bill C-133, an amendment proposed by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) to change from 6 per cent to 6.5 per cent and from 5 per cent to 5.5 per cent the indexing of pensions of retired public servants. I am opposing the motion and my Party is opposing the amendment because it is wrong.
Yesterday evening when I was speaking on the Bill I pointed out that a deal is a deal is a deal. The deal which was made between the public servants of Canada, their pension fund and their pension future, with the Government of Canada was a deal. When the deal was finished both sides believed that it was sincere and true. Unfortunately, we find out now that the Government did not accept it as a deal and has decided to change it. We are speaking against that kind of thing because it is wrong.
Public servants have paid into this pension fund in all good faith and with the good will that when their time came to retire they would be receiving the pensions which had been prescribed to them by the negotiations and the deal made with the Government. Unfortunately, that deal has been broken. This brings to the fore of my mind one of the most serious problems that we as Members of Parliament face in the House of Commons. That is, who are we to believe and who are the people of Canada to believe? I stand here and people judge me for my credibility; do I speak or do 1 not speak the truth? My colleagues on all sides of the House have the same responsibility. They stand before this House of Commons and before the people of Canada. They do so whether they are credible or not. I have talked to many people in Canada and I believe that many Canadians are losing their faith in this House and in the value of this House of Commons. One of the reasons for that is broken deals.
All of us must ask ourselves the question: "Are we credible?" I have to do that, Members of my Party must, and so must Members of the Conservative Party and the Liberal
Party ask themselves. That question must be asked by Members of the Cabinet and by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). We must ask ourselves whether we are credible; are we telling the truth; are we doing what we say? If we cannot answer yes to those questions, then I have a moral responsibility to myself, and others in this House of Commons have a moral responsibility to themselves, to do something about it.
Unfortunately, the people of Canada, the voters out there, do not have the force of power to come here and argue their case in the House. We have to do it for them. But 1 know when I speak about the broken deal on the civil servants' pension fund that I speak what they are saying and what they are thinking.
We have legislation before us now that has been so easily summarized under the catch phrase "six and five". This six and five program is a sort of direction or thrust that was thrown out to the Canadian people as a solution to their problems. My colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party, by supporting that direction, should stand up now and say that having supported the direction they therefore support this amendment, because that is the truth. If you buy a principle, then you buy what the principle says you have to do.
I am asking the President of the Treasury Board to reconsider seriously what he has proposed. I am asking the Government to reconsider seriously what it has proposed in these Bills that are now being bound around the six and five principle.
I think it is important as we debate this particular Bill to remember that as people get more power and more financial strength they have a more difficult time speaking the truth all the time. I believe that poor people who tell you that they are hungry, that they cannot look after themselves in their old age, that they are sick or that they do not have a job, will speak the truth more clearly and more frequently. That is easily understood. It is not a new idea; it is as old as the biblical traditions that we have. Those who become powerful and rich-I speak of governments, of the House of Commons, of business people, of labour unions, of anybody who becomes powerful and rich and gets away from the poor-have a great deal of difficulty in speaking the truth all the time.
Today, as I throw in my few words on this important amendment and Bill, I ask that the Government seriously reconsider what it has done. I ask Members of this House of Commons to consider seriously what they have done. We should cancel those Bills. If that does not happen, I can say very clearly that what is going to happen in the next election in Windsor is that the campaign slogan will be "Goodbye, Herb".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin my remarks at the report stage of Bill C-133, which amends the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act and adversely affects public servants' pensions, by underlying the massive implications of this measure for Canadian pensioners and public workers.

January 18, 1983

First, the 6 per cent and 5 per cent cap on pension increases directly affects 200,000 public servants who can rightly claim that they bargained and paid for this benefit. The fact that this employment agreement was entrenched in the statute law and can only be changed by a parliamentary Act is evidence of this social contract.
Second, there are 500,000 public servants employed by the Government of Canada and its agencies, including the Canadian Armed Forces and the RCMP, who view this legislative change as adversely affecting their pension rights and benefits.
Third, this Bill, C-133, involves a breach of faith for every Canadian because every Canadian who receives a benefit under the statute law of the Parliament of Canada cannot rest assured that that benefit will be continued in all circumstances.
The Government has taken the position that if it considers it necessary in the interest of its financial responsibility to remove benefits without consultation, without prior discussion with the beneficiaries, it can do so by simply introducing an amending Bill in the House of Commons. That is a breach of faith which should concern not only the 700,000 public servants who are particularly affected by this Bill, but it is a breach of faith which should concern all Canadians.
I am certain that every one of the 700,000 responsible and socially conscious Canadians who are represented by the retired public servants and by those now in the Canadian Public Service would accept a limit on their statutory pension rights if that limit was based on reality and principle. However, the Government has substituted fiction for facts. The Government has replaced principle with prejudice.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his Cabinet colleagues have systematically and maliciously created a false impression of the federal public servant and, in the case of Bill C-133, the retired public servant. That perception first projects a retired public servant as one who is given pension benefits as an unearned reward by an overgenerous employer. Second, this fictional public servant was overpaid for most of his or her working life, yet the retirement benefit was a substantial percentage-as much as 70 per cent-of that bloated salary. Third, the overpaid and undeserving senior citizens scoff at high inflation rates because, in fact, according to the Government, senior citizens benefit from that inflation rate because the pension income they receive is increased in line with the cost of living.
To suggest to the Canadian people that retired public servants benefit from inflation and therefore can accept a cap on that benefit is ridiculous. What a tragedy it is that well informed Canadians would accept such a false and deceptive description of the retired public servant. What a tragedy that our Prime Minister and his Cabinet colleagues would, with malice aforethought, create such a perception for the public to accept. This is moral bankruptcy at its lowest level.
The Prime Minister and his colleagues who hold a majority in this House will make Bill C-133 the law of this land, but
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act {No. 2)
they will not suceed in convincing Canadians that their action is right and just.
Why is this Act not right? Because the whole six and five program is a fraud and a sham. It is a public fraud on the Canadian people. The Government continues to spend at the rate it has spent over the last decade. It continues to build up a deficit which is now at $23 billion. We were told this very week that it is going up to $30 billion.
Why is Bill C-133 unjust? Because there are 200,000 pensioners who have an average income of $6,900 a year. When one adds the old age assistance to this income, a retired public servant 65 years of age or over, if he has a wife, is below the poverty line of $10,400.
Let me look at the specific problems that are encountered by aging Canadians. In some cases they require care in a nursing home or a similar institution. There is no way that a retired public servant whose income averages $6,900, even with the old age assistance benefit, can pay for nursing care in a nursing home institution anywhere in Canada. Our retired public servants who have spent their working lives trying to provide for their old age are deprived of the financial ability, in most cases, to pay even for nursing care in an institutionalized setting. Therefore, to call the action being taken in Bill C-133 fair or just is to defeat the purpose of those expressions.
I question whether the measure is necessary. The saving to the public purse, as I understand it, will be $15 million in this fiscal year and $85 million in the subsequent fiscal year because of the change which will be brought about by the provisions of Bill C-133. I have already pointed out that the Government continues its spending at an alarming rate and is piling up an even greater deficit than that projected in the June, 1982 Budget which created the six and five program. However, let me give some other examples of Government spending, which are in excess of $100 million, which will be saved by the provisions of Bill C-133.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is in the House and I am sure he is about to approve the construction of a vessel to ply between Nova Scotia and Newfoundland and span the Gulf. The estimated cost of that vessel is $122 million and the project was first rejected by the Government. It is now apparently being reinstated, not to help the poor people in Newfoundland or in Nova Scotia but, rather, to help the company that will build the vessel, a subsidiary of Dome Petroleum, the Davie Shipbuilding Company. So there is $122 million which will be spent.

The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) has had the courage of his convictions in this matter. As a matter of fact, I want to commend him for having the courage of his convictions as opposed to his fellow sheep on the back bench of the Liberal Party who have abandoned their constituents on this particular issue. I have had several of my constituents write to me or call me, both civil servants and non-civil servants, asking that I put forward their views on this particular amendment.
There are two points that I wish to make briefly. One is that the people of Simcoe North, my constituents, believe that a deal is a deal, that an agreement, once made, should not be broken unilaterally. That is exactly what the Liberal Government has done in this Bill. They have broken an agreement which they made with the civil servants of this country. Secondly, the people of Simcoe North believe that the Government should not fight inflation on the backs of those who cannot fight back.
What I want to do for a moment is to elaborate on both of these points. Several years ago the federal Government agreed to index civil servants' pensions to cover the effect of inflation. That meant that each year there would be an increase in the pension paid to a civil servant to allow for the inflation of the previous year, if any. The theory was that the recipient would always be in the same position as he or she was guaranteed under the agreement made with the Government. Pensions would be indexed to inflation.

What the Government is doing in this Bill and what our amendment attempts to correct, or stop for a period of time, is to index pensions only so much as the Government wishes; in other words, to index only to 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984.
The Government entered into an agreement collectively, with the union-and I suggest it entered into it individually with each and every civil servant-to index pensions to inflation. On the other side of the agreement, the union agreed, and each individual member of the union agreed, that they would pay a premium for that indexing. As I understand it, that is 1 per cent of salary.

Mr. Speaker, I want to put a few comments on the record respecting Bill C-133 and the matter of the superannuated pension. It was previously asked whether the six and five program should have been supported originally. My answer is yes. It not only gave a signal to both the public and private community that inflation was a major problem in the economy, but the Government had to recognize it and come to grips with it. As has been mentioned, because of recessionary factors and pressures there is no question that the reduction in inflation has been influenced largely by that rather than any government program.
Bill C-133 is quite different from Bill C-124 which was a capping of salaries of public servants, 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year. That was the essence of Bill C-124. The merit of those two proposals is evident and I do not have to make further comment on that.
When we get to deal with Bill C-133, we are in a different situation. I will explain it in this way. On the one hand, Canadians through their tax dollars pay money into general revenues at the federal, provincial and municipal levels. Those moneys are used to provide services which those Governments, Parliament or the legislatures decide to be important for the well-being of the general population.
We as Opposition Members and as members of society generally might argue that the Government is not using those funds in the best way possible. Through the methods in this House, namely by debate and eventually by the electoral process, the Canadian people give their verdict as to whether the Government of the day has prudently spent the tax dollars collected by Government over the course of the years.
That is a process we all understand. The question of accountability is central. However, when we look at money which has been received by individuals, money deducted at source when people receive their salary cheques or money directly paid to a pension plan, that money is very different from general revenues. General revenues are moneys used for the general well-being of society. When an individual Canadian pays a premium for a pension to be received at the time of retirement, that money is held in trust by the Government to make it work to the best advantage of those who initially contributed to that pension plan. It is a trust fund. Therefore, that money should be seen by Governments differently from the general pool which is often referred to as the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
The Government has an obligation to fulfil the terms of the pension agreement. What we are dealing with today is a pension agreement between the Government and every public servant who has contributed his or her pension premium to a pension plan. They do not know what the pay-out will be at the time of retirement. It depends on the salary earned and the number of years of contribution and, until the passage of this Bill, on the so-called escalation which is related to the cost of living increase.
Because of the power it has in the House of Commons, the Government says it will now change that agreement. I believe that is wrong. The people who contributed to the pension fund
are now being told that the other partner, the Government of Canada, is changing the rules. Ironically it is only one partner that can change the rules because of the power that partner has in this House of Commons through the legislative process. Previously the rules were changed through the collective bargaining system by agreement. What we are dealing with today is an agreement between the Government and the public servant.
Over the past number of days all of us have had experience with people who are concerned about their investment. As I spoke to my constituents during the Christmas break, I found a certain attitude. They were willing to invest and have the money to invest, but they had great fears along the following lines. First, would the Government change the tax rules again if they made an investment today? Would the rules again change at the time of the next Budget? That creates real confusion in the mind of the average person who wants to invest, create jobs and make the economy go.
Second, and I found this interesting, they were concerned about the viability of Canada's financial institutions. The average person was asking whether his money would be safe and secure. I do not want to comment today on what is happening in the Ontario legislature relative to mortgage and trust companies, but it has not helped that attitude. It has created even more confusion and fear. Fear is not too strong a word in this regard. The average person wants to know whether his investment will be secure. For example, in Winnipeg there are some branches of the Ontario companies that are involved. Average people stood in line in the cold of winter in Winnipeg to see whether their investment was secure, the financial future in which they had invested.
When dealing with Bill C-133, we must also touch on the human factors. Individuals believe that if they work and do their job properly and contribute at a certain rate, they will have a certain pension not only for themselves but, more important, for their families when they pass on. These people have contributed an extra percentage point to buy escalation in pension equal to the cost of living increase. Nowhere in the legislation are these people given the option of not having to pay the extra 1 per cent.
I find it very difficult to understand how the Government can say: "Well, we are not going to escalate in to the cost of living; and, secondly, we still expect you to pay the premium which bought that protection". I do not think a private insurance company could get away with that. It they said, when one bought either a life insurance policy, superannuation or whatever, "Look, those were the conditions but we have decided to change them even though you signed a contract", I would think the Government would step in very quickly and say very specifically: "You have a contract, fulfil it". There might also be a question from the general public as to whether the fund is solvent. But I think if you look at the surplus in the fund, that question is answered as well.
January 18, 1983

The last point I want to make, from my constituents' point of view, is this. It is generally regarded that there are not that many public servants in my riding, active or retired. Well, that is simply not the case in a riding where there are five border crossings or where there is a community, Whiteshell-Pinawa, which has an atomic energy research station. I have before me, Mr. Speaker, a petition signed by some 200 people from communities such as Pinawa, Beausejour, Whitemouth, River Hills, Lac du Bonnet, Seven Sisters Falls, Winnipeg, Elma, Seddon's Corner, Tyndall and Transcona who said: "We paid in, signed a contract and we are living up to our contract; members of the Government, live up to your side of it as well". That is the message they have given to me and that is the message I have given to the House.
The reduction of inflation is a valid national goal, but when you have a contract and you expect other Canadians to live up to their side of the contract, I suggest the Government, for its own integrity, do the same thing.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, welcome the opportunity of being able to participate in this most important debate. It is something 1 really do not enjoy, however, because of the fact that I find Bill C-133 to be one of the most repugnant pieces of legislation to be introduced in the House since I have been here.
As speaker after speaker from both opposition parties has indicated, this Bill is breaking a contract between the Government and its past and present employees. It destroys an agreement, something which would not be allowed in the private sector. It is morally and economically wrong. Essentially what it does is cap at the 6.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent level the increase in pensions of some 154,367 retired public servants who receive an average pension of some S6,900 a year. They will receive an increase in their pension of 0.5 per cent more than mothers or people on Old Age Security because of a sense of guilt by the Government over the fact that these people have paid into a fund and are indeed entitled to full indexation because they won it in contract negotiations.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Government can claim that the net effect is not going to be all that great because inflation is going to be down next year, perhaps even to 6 per cent. We all hope it will be, but that is not the point. The point is that retired civil servants have fought for and won the right to some protection in periods of rapid economic change. They have paid for it. There is no guarantee, Mr. Speaker, of what the inflation rate will be during the next two years. When we look at the economic forecasts during the last two years, what sticks out is that nobody knows what in heaven's name is going on. All the predictions have been wrong-predictions as to what is happening with the economy, when the recovery is going to occur, what Government deficits are going to be, what inflation or unemployment is going to be. Economists, both in the private and public sector, have been unable to make any accurate, long-term predictions. No one can tell us with any degree of certainty what the inflation rate is going to be next year, yet Bill C-133 removes the protection against inflation for the very people who need that protection the most. The
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
only protection people such as mothers or the retired have is what they have legally gained through institutions such as Parliament. But the Government removes this protection in the name of fighting inflation. That is insanity and cynicism from the Government opposite which just amazes me. It is wrong economics.
The Conference Board of Canada stated last week, and I quote from The Globe and Mail of January 13, 1983:
-the recovery will continue to be hampered by the weak growth expected in real disposable income in 1983.
Essentially the Board says that while consumer confidence is high in Canada, the ability of Canadians to purchase the goods and services they want and need is hampered by the fact that they do not have the purchasing power, and the cutbacks introduced by the Government and massive unemployment are preventing economic recovery. This proposed legislation, Mr. Speaker, further aggravates the basic problem. We are not going to get on the road to economic recovery with legislation like Bill C-133. In fact, this Bill further slows down the economy. I am not certain that there is an explanation for why the Government cannot see or understand this. Perhaps it does. Perhaps it is quite willing cynically to say: "This is the price we are prepared to pay to wrestle inflation to the ground. We are prepared to see old age pensioners, mothers, and retired civil servants squeezed even further in order to fight inflation to the ground."
We in the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, have maintained from day one that this type of Reaganomics will not work. The amount of human suffering is too great to make this an acceptable cure for inflation. In fact, this type of Reaganomics will lead to economic disaster, bankruptcies, massive unemployment and, perhaps, to the very ruin and crash of our present economic system.
I was definitely encouraged to hear Members of the Conservative Party denounce this legislation because it broke contracts. They spoke in terms of the importance of understanding and of gentlemen's agreements on contracts. They are absolutely correct, but I sense a bit of a double standard there because they supported Bill C-124 which capped salaries of public servants. That Bill broke a lot of contracts that had been negotiated between public servants and their employer, the Government, yet we only heard two Members of the Conservative Party protest that obnoxious Bill C-124.
I think the Conservative Party still has a chance to show how sincere its opposition is to Bills C-131, 132 and 133. Members will meet in convention next week. I challenge them to introduce and pass a resolution at that convention that would denounce Bills C-131, C-132 and C-133. If at that convention they pass resolutions condemning those pieces of legislation, then some of the faith that I used to have in that Party will be restored. I challenge its Members to introduce such a motion and to marshal it through the convention next week.

January 18, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act {No. 2)

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now engaged in what has become the longest parliamentary session in Canadian history, and this so shortly after a Christmas recess when one might have thought Members of the Government, if they had listened to their constituents, would have returned with fresh, new ideas about how to fight inflation. But they have not, so we must continue our opposition to their approach to the battle against inflation.
Bill C-133 is more than just mean-minded. It comes at what is perhaps the blackest moment in Canada's pension history. Goodness knows what will follow. Should Government backbenchers see fit to fall into line and vote for the legislation, they will be playing a major role in this blackest moment in our history.
In the name of restraint, the Government has chosen to launch a stubborn and determined attack on senior citizens, mothers and Public Service employees while it just as steadfastly refuses to put its own house in order and curtail Government expenditures.
Who are the people who are being asked to make sacrifices as a result of Bill C-133? It certainly is not Senator Pitfield or Edmund Clark. Some 70 per cent of the people affected by this Bill are receiving pensions of less than $10,000 per year. Better than 80 per cent of widows and survivors of public servants receive pensions of under $5,000 per year. Are these the people whose inflationary expectations must be brought into line? Are these people to be made an example of for the Canadian people?
It was suggested at second reading of the Bill that the Government could be sympathetic enough at least to exclude pensioners in the lower income brackets. The response was that pensioners in the lower income brackets could not be excluded because there were too many of them. That response speaks volumes about the insensitivity of Members across the floor.
These are tough times, the Government says. Tough times, indeed, Mr. Speaker, for those persons who cannot bear the brunt of this inflationary attack. Do Members across the floor not realize that never in Canadian history, not even in the darkest hours of the depression of the thirties, has a Government altered pension arrangements as is proposed now? That has never happened, Mr. Speaker. This action is totally unprecedented. It is disgraceful, it is shameful and it should not take place. It breaks trust and it certainly destroys confidence. It is bad enough that a Government should attempt to build a restraint program on the backs of pensioners without taking them into consideration and the fact that it is establishing a bald-faced precedent.
1 was raised to believe, and my children have been brought up as well to believe, that my word is my bond. A deal is a deal. As a lawyer, I was persuaded many times to put a deal
into writing. What does the Government propose? It does not matter that the Government's agreement has been reduced to a convention and an understanding that public servants could retire on a contributory pension which, they were told in 1974, would be indexed. This Bill not only unilaterally breaks that deal, but it does so without prior consultation and without prior notice. Such action, whether it be in the Public Service or the private sector, can only lead to bad relations between management and labour.
In trying to resolve all the issues that arose in the formulation of the Civil Service Staff Relations Act, the Public Service unions and associations agreed to forfeit the right to bargain pensions in return for an agreement on the part of the Government of the day that it would never tamper with Public Service pensions without full and meaningful consultation. This agreement obtained through 1971, when partial indexing was adopted, to 1974, when full indexing was introduced, and onward until June, 1982 when the Government broke it without notice and without consultation.
Throughout the period from 1967 to June 1982 it was understood that it was the Government's responsibility to administer the pension fund and, from 1981, the indexation account, in an actuarially sound manner. The Government was to set the contributory rate in consultation with the staff associations and unions; it was to match that rate and, most important in the context of Bill C-133, it was to make up any deficiencies that might result. Public servants, in turn, were to pay that which was agreed upon, namely 1 per cent of gross earnings, for indexation. How the Government chose to invest the pension and indexation funds was the business of the Government, not of the unions or associations.
Now, out of the blue, the Government is breaking the agreement made 15 years ago with respect to changes in the area of pensions and it is making a mockery of the 1974 promise to provide full indexation. To add insult to injury, the Government is justifying this by pointing to its own less than satisfactory investment and accounting practices and to the good faith and trust extended by the unions and associations of the Public Service in not insisting upon a formal contract.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-133 is a contemptible and repugnant piece of legislation. It attacks those who have no way to defend themselves, those who are in no position to fight inflation themselves. They are being asked to bear the brunt of the Government's attack on pension legislation. These pensioners are not only going to lose, on average, some $1,200 over the two-year period that the program will be in place, but they will see their pension base eroded by an estimated 10 per cent for the balance of their pension life.
The amendment put forward by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) is not only inadequate, it is an insult to the intelligence and integrity of Public Service pensioners. The honourable course, Mr. Speaker, is to defeat the Bill or to withdraw it.
January 18, 1983

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to have this opportunity today to rise and speak on this aspect of Bill C-133, not because it is a good Bill, but because it provides one with an opportunity to speak on this very dark day in Canadian pension history. It allows a person to raise on behalf of tens of thousands of Canadians a number of issues which they would dearly love to raise before the Government of Canada themselves. They have requested that the Members of Parliament who represent them do it on their behalf.
Over the last number of weeks, during the Christmas recess especially, 1 had the opportunity to meet with retired public servants, retired members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and retired members of Canada's Armed Forces. They approached me both formally and informally to ask just what on earth the Government of Canada was doing. These three areas of Canada's Public Service were under the impression that they had entered into a contract with the Government of Canada, that they had made an arrangement or a deal, and that there was a clear understanding.
I am referring, for example, to those public servants who had really committed themselves and dedicated their lives to being public servants in the most positive aspect of that term, those who had literally established careers and dedicated their lives to serving Canadians and Canada. I am referring to such people as those who for years and years represented us as a country in our Customs houses and immigration offices here and abroad, those who represented Canada in weather stations both in the settled parts of Canada and often in very remote areas of the country, those who dedicated their lives to assisting the unemployed through UIC offices, those in Parks Canada who served the public, protected wildlife and made more inaccessible areas of Canada a welcome part of Canada's heritage. They welcomed people into those parks and introduced them to the finer elements of our environment and Canadian ecology. Also I am referring to people in fisheries who often risked their lives working for that very critical resource industry. One could go on and on referring to people who dedicated their lives to serving Canada.
Retired members of the Armed Forces have come to me and said, "Mr. Riis, as my Member of Parliament, I want to tell you that 1 have dedicated my life to this country." They say that in a way different from other Canadians. In fact, they served in World War II and literally laid their lives on the line on many, many occasions. They were prepared to risk their lives for Canada. They served Canada in Korea and in a number of peace-keeping missions around the world. When they got up in the morning and went out on the job, they were prepared to give their lives for Canada as a result of a contract into which they had entered between themselves and the Government of Canada. Also I refer to those members of the RCMP who daily, year after year, decade after decade, risked their lives to protect Canadian citizens in whatever part of Canada they were found. From the largest metropolitan areas to the most remote coasts, RCMP members were prepared to
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
dedicate their lives and in many cases risk their lives frequently on Canada's behalf.
These people had an understanding. In many cases they virtually had a contract that their service would be recognized in their pensions. The pension is not excessive; a typical retired public servant receives today $6,900. They recognized that there was a factor of inflation which would jeopardize that pension. They were given the opportunity to pay into a fund which would protect them in the case of inflation. The Government of Canada indicated that that should be included as part of the understanding of the deal being made, that not only would they contribute 6 per cent toward their pension but they would add another percentage point to protect them against the ravages of inflation. Many of them decided that they would retire early for two reasons-to allow access to their career for other Canadians and because they knew they would be protected in the case of rapid inflationary growth.
Now they have learned through one source or another that the Government has turned its back on them and has decided to change the contract, to renege on the contract, to break the contract. They are puzzled. They really cannot believe that the Government for which they worked for many years-people who had literally dedicated their lives to serving Canada, Canadians and the Government of Canada-was now turning its back on them.
We have heard other speakers refer to the crisis in leadership confidence. I read with interest in The Globe and Mail this morning one of Canada's best columnists, who identified that our critical problem today was that Canadians had lost confidence in their leadership for good reasons. The article indicated that they cannot trust the leadership of the Government of Canada any longer, that the leadership says one thing and does another. An example of that is that the Government of Canada entered into a contract with its public servants and now it has broken it.
Also the columnist referred to the Progressive Conservative Party. I suspect many people are perplexed when Members of the Progressive Conservative Party rose and said that they supported the six and five principle and were prepared to break contracts with tens of thousands of Canadians. Now they rise and say that they do not like breaking certain contracts with certain aspects of the Public Service of Canada. Then the people of Canada ask, "What on earth does the Progressive Conservative Party stand for; where is its integrity? It is prepared to break some contracts but is hesitant to break this one."
I must say that there are some Members of the Progressive Conservative Party who have a heart, a conscience and integrity. Those are the ones who stood in their places and said, "We will not participate in this hypocritical move in which the rest of our colleagues in the Conservative Party are participating." They had the courage to stand up and say that.
I believe it must be said very clearly that there is a crisis of leadership confidence in the country, and that the Liberal Party of Canada and the Progressive Conservative Party of

Canada are providing ample fuel for that speculation. Canadian public servants are truly confused when they find the contracts into which they had entered being broken and in principle supported by the Conservatives as well.
The disappointing aspect of Bill C-133 is really twofold. One is that it fights inflation on the backs of those people who are really the victims of inflation. If there is one group in Canada feeling the pinch of inflation, it has to be those on fixed incomes, especially those who are retired. The Government says that those who are suffering the most and are paying the greatest penalty will be those people on whose backs it will fight this war as well. They are the casualties of the war. Simply, this Bill will add to the casualty list in terms of people who are suffering as a result of the six and five program. Most important, we must recognize that Bill C-133 breaks contracts. When they start breaking contracts, confidence begins to erode and any support which the political leadership had created in the months previous quickly evaporates, and I suspect it has been totally evaporated at this point.
I call upon all those Members of Parliament in this House to stand up and be counted when the vote comes. I say to Liberal backbenchers: "Have the courage to represent not only your constituents but have the integrity to represent those people across this country who have literally dedicated their lives to the service of Canada". I am thinking of those people in the Armed Forces, in the RCMP and those dedicated public servants who have given up their lives to serve Canada. The least we can do now is to give them a fair pension.

Mr. Speaker, much has been stated here in the House and during sittings of the Miscellaneous Estimates Committee as it heard witnesses who appeared to give their reaction, almost universally adverse, to Bill C-133. Much has been stated that reflects very poorly on the Government of Canada breaking trust with its employees and retirees in the matter of indexation of pensions.
Certainly of all the witnesses who appeared representing the many elements of the Public Service in Canada, the breaking of a trust relationship dominated their testimony. In addition, we have all received letters and communications from constituents whose interests are adversely affected by Bill C-133. Typical is a letter received recently from Mr. William Hitchen of Victoria, B.C., who is chairman of the Organization for Indexed Pensions. In his letter he writes:
The Prime Minister has recently made a plea for trust between Canadians. Pillaging the funded Public Service pension accounts does not improve trust.
Please help to defeat Bill C-133.
Mr. Hitchen also wrote:
Bill C-133 is designed to limit the indexing of Public Service pensions to 6 per cent and 5 per cent over the next two years. Its purpose obviously is to enhance the Government's "six and five" program, although in actual fact its implementation would contribute practically nothing to our fight on inflation.
On that point I believe it is clear we have to take issue with what our colleagues to my left have repeatedly been saying about the Progressive Conservative Party's position concerning
Bill C-124. Bill C-124 was the first indication that the Government of Canada took the damage that inflation was doing to our citizens seriously. It was on the basis that Bill C-124 was the first move by the Government of Canada to do something about it that we supported Bill C-124. Up to that point the Government had not taken seriously the damage it was inflicting on the economy of Canada and to individual Canadian citizens. The Government was then seen to recognize what was happening. Because Bill C-124 was the first step toward bringing Government activity under control, we supported it. But we have been offended by the repeated actions of this Government that have gone against the spirit of Bill C-124. Canadians right across the country have been offended by what is seen as the failure of the Government to live up to its commitment which it gave to the Canadian people when it put the problems that inflation were producing before them and produced as a first step toward resolving those problems Bill C-124.
I asked a witness who appeared before the Committee whether that person would be ready to accept the implication of Bill C-133 if an awareness was reflected in Government action day by day that it, the Government, was the prime producer of inflation in Canada, a problem that could only be brought under control by trimming its own voracious appetite for spending. The witness's response was: "Yes, indeed, it would be more palatable if the burden were shared right across the spectrum of society".
The problem is unequal treatment. That is what offends Canadians. For example, the generosity extended to Mr. Pitfield stands in marked contrast to the treatment of pensioners whose average pension is less than $7,000 annually. Naturally, they are offended when they read of the generous spirit shown to a public servant who has served Canada well, I am sure, but whose situation stands in marked contrast to that of the ordinary pensioner and superannuate.
The generosity of this Government to its friends, as demonstrated by the Maislin trucking bail-out and by the selection of Mr. Erikson to design the embassy in Washington, by-passing the expensive and thorough selection committee recommendations, offends Canadians. These actions stand in contrast to the way superannuates are being treated. All those things offend me and they offend the Canadian public.
What about the $17 million grant to the Holiday Inn to build a hotel in the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce's riding in the city of Windsor? It is interesting to note that Minister is now President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) and has responsibility for Bill C-133. That action stands in marked contrast to what the Government is asking, which is a denial of a privilege that was guaranteed to superannuates and is now being taken away from them through Bill C-133.
What about the several hundreds of millions of dollars being spent on Government advertising? I see the Government's present information budget is $235 million. The federal Government has risen from being the seventeenth largest advertiser in Canada to being the largest advertiser in Canada.
January 18, 1983

Surely if we are looking at places to trim Government spending we can point the finger to more productive sources of saving. We should not be looking to the pensioners and superannuates, the people who have contributed far more funds than have been taken out. Surely we can look to those sources. The traditional role of Government spending has been to provide information but it has gone far beyond that process now. It is not information that the Government is providing, it is soliciting support for programs and Government initiatives, many of which are not worthy of support.
You have indicated to me that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. 1 just wish to say on behalf of those who appeared as witnesses before the Committee that the Government can make all people appreciate the effect of restraint by demonstrating restraint itself. This would bring all the people on the side of the Government in the matter of restraint. We will not be supporting this Bill, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some weeks ago at an earlier stage in this debate I made my fundamental objections to this and the other pieces of legislation quite clear. Over the years the question of my parliamentary responsibility has never been a complicated one for me. If a piece of legislation is good law, then it should be supported. If it lacks that qualification, it should be opposed. I have always believed that good laws were simply those which the people in fact wanted to support and embraced as being for the betterment of themselves, their community, the country and the world.
I do not have any difficulty in deciding upon this series of legislation which has been introduced in support of the principles of the six and five program. I have opposed it since the beginning. While the particular measure in front of us now could be improved with the Government's acceptance of certain amendments, I am somewhat amazed to believe that the Government would continue in the perpetration of this hoax.
Our economy is in a serious recession. There is a growing consensus, from what I have read, that it is just such measures as this which effectively take spending money out of the market place that will, in fact, prolong the very recession that the Government claims measures such as this will cure. I believe the Government has admitted this fact to some extent, perhaps simply to smooth over the objections of some of their more thoughtful supporters. The Government has admitted its error in this legislation by sneaking in this amendment for 5.5 per cent and 6.5 per cent. However, it makes no impact at all.
The Government should be determining ways to inject real dollars into the economy which will provide the capital pool for those manufacturers, processors and developers in this country to sell their goods and services and therefore enable them to rehire workers and get the industrial effort in this country back on track. This is poor legislation, if for no other reason than that. However, the problem is much more complex than this simple test for what a responsible Member of Parliament
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
should do with respect to the principle of what is good or bad legislation.
One can consider this legislation from the point of view of being a very personal attack on the retirement capacity of people to live with some degree of dignity. We are aware that the savings to the Government are immeasureably small. The Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) cited only two or three examples. He is quite right that there are literally hundreds of examples which could be cited. The average pension income is still under $7,000 and Old Age Security is still under $3,000. The total income which pensioners receive presently is below the poverty line. This is a fact which is acknowledged and accepted by everyone.
If this program was to result in the recovery of sufficient amounts of money to restore economic activity in the country, there would then be some basis on which to listen to the arguments of the Government for support for this program. However, this is not the case. The Government is taking money from an already hard hit group of people. In Nova Scotia, we have 15,000 retired federal public servants. In Halifax-Dartmouth alone there are 37,000 public sector employees. What will they live on when they retire? The domestic electricity rates in Nova Scotia have just risen by 28 per cent. You know in your own Province, Mr. Speaker, how domestic electrical costs compare to the national average. Despite this one increased item alone, the Government will remove even more funds from these people.
I reject this legislation because I believe we should be in an expansionary mood in the House instead of a contracting posture. We have seen a bleak year in 1982 which we may wish to forget. However, when we look ahead in 1983 the picture is not much better and this type of legislation will do nothing to help that forecast.
The employment rate has fallen for 16 consecutive months, with 492,000 fewer identifiable jobs than there were a year ago. We know there are 1.5 million people unemployed and I am sure there are another 750,000 unemployed people who cannot be identified or counted. This legislation does nothing to address the problems faced by them.
Some 10,000 businesses have been pushed into bankruptcy in recent months. It is no wonder that inflation is dropping, since there is theoretically no money while national productivity is running between 60 per cent and 65 per cent in terms of efficiency. We know what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said in this respect. Perhaps we will soon have 100 per cent efficiency with no firms operating at all. If that is the direction in which the Government is heading, it may be able to produce some good statistics from that.
This is poor legislation which should not be supported. The difficulty with the legislative process in this place is that, once there is a commitment to a particular course of action, there is no fundamental sense of responsibility to change direction. We simply forge on with it, whether rightly or wrongly. "Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!" The Government is torpedoing a whole segment of Canadian society which, the good Lord knows, are presently facing enough difficulty in making ends meet without having this further burden imposed upon them.

January 18, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
There are amendments which should be made to this legislation, the very least of which should be a sunset law to bring it to an end. These things are apparently not acceptable to the Government. I do not even know for sure whether it has even considered them. If in fact inflation does not come down, does the Government hold out any hope to these people that money taken away from them by this measure can be given back to them to help restore them to a level at least approaching dignity?
Indexing is a principle which was introduced in this Chamber by a former leader of ours, the Hon. Robert Stanfield. subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak on the so-called compromise amendment to Bill C-133. To start off, I would like to tell the rest of the story about the Conservative support for Bill C-124. The Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King) spent a considerable amount of his ten-minute speech explaining how the Conservatives had been tricked into supporting Bill C-124, but they could not follow through on that support in the Bills which came to follow. In speaking against the Bill, they argued that it is wrong for the Government to break contracts and that deals which have been made are deals which should be kept. How hypocritical can one get, Mr. Speaker?
Bill C-124 broke many negotiated, signed contracts established by recognized unions which had fought long and hard for the benefits which those contracts gave to them. The Progressive Conservatives supported that Bill. Now for the sake of political expediency, they are against this Bill. We accept their support. We are glad that the superannuates have their support and that, in the process, if Hon. Members across the way are able to get up the courage and vote as they would probably like to vote, we may be able to defeat this Bill. However, let the people of Canada realize that the Conservative Party here is being selective as to what contracts it will support and what contracts it will break. Let there be no suggestion that just because its Members supported Bill C-124, they have good reason to vote against Bill C-133.
The Government has presented a number of Bills, the six and five Bills, and has said that it does not really need these
Bills. What it is trying to do is to work on the psychological impact of inflation. That sounds like a pretty good idea, but who contributes to inflation? It certainly is not the superannuates. It certainly is not the workers, farmers, or small businessmen. These people are now receiving less to live on than they did a year ago or even five years ago. They are not the people who are contributing to inflation. Farmers from my district are receiving 17 per cent to 25 per cent less income this year than they did last year. Superannuates are receiving real wages or real retirement benefits which are comparatively less than they were two years ago, and this 6 per cent does not increase them to a level which is equal to inflation.
We should take a good look at who contributes to inflation. There is a story which all of us know, the story of Alice in Wonderland, where the Queen tells Alice: "Look, you must run as fast as you can so that you can stay in one place". That is what the superannuates are trying to do. Here we have the Government stating that although it did make an agreement a number of years ago, and although there was a handshake on it and everyone accepted the fact that the Government would support indexed pensions, suddenly it is in the position where it will no longer keep the agreement.
The Government is almost symbolic of one which will go ahead and break contracts and break the law in the process of attempting to put before the people a rather unacceptable point of view. Let us consider the record of the Government in breaking contracts. This particular Bill would break contracts with civil servants and the amendment is a compromise. What a compromise! It amounts to an increase of .5 per cent, or $39 a year for the average civil servant.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is present in the House. He has proposed before this House, before the people of Canada, the breaking of a contract which was established in 1925.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the amendments before us is to cap the amount of the increase under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act at a level substantially less than the present rate of inflation would require. I think the very fact that this objective has been set out so clearly would be an incentive for every Member in this House to oppose this measure. As we look at it a little further, we realize that those affected are federal Public Service superannuates, including members of the Armed Forces and the RCMP.
We are all aware of the tremendous contribution these individuals have made to Canada and Canadians. Federal public servants have served in a very effective and commendable manner throughout the past years. Members of the Armed Forces have shown their ability and willingness to sacrifice everything in the interests of our country. The RCMP have a record that is not surpassed by any agency in the world. Yet the Government states that this is the way in which we are going to reward them for their contribution toward the welfare of Canada and the benefit of Canadians.
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
To my mind, this is one of the most reprehensible proposals that has ever been made in this House of Commons. Is this the way to treat those who have given the very best of their lives to serve our interests? I would say it is a jolt to the faith of all those who are affected by it. They believed that in rendering this service to Canadians, and in view of the agreements and understandings which had been entered into, they could trust the Government, that they could trust those in authority to see to it that their remuneration or their superannuation was at least a reasonable amount, and they believed that the commitments made would be honoured. This is a real jolt to their faith in Government, which actually constitutes their employer. It is a jolt to their sense of security because they have no doubt considered, as we all have, the days when our participation in the active labour force will come to a close. They were depending on their pensions and they believed their future was guaranteed. With the introduction of a Bill such as the one before us, their confidence has been shattered, their faith has been severely jeopardized and their confidence in their employer and in their country has suffered a real setback.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon), placed on record yesterday an excerpt from a letter signed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I just want to read the relevant section here. My colleague quoted this letter as follows:
In our society, pensions provide a means of sharing risk so that we can retire in reasonable security and dignity, without fear of the future. Protecting pensions from inflation by indexing them to increases in the cost of living should be an integral part of our pension schemes. Indexing does not give pensioners an increasingly larger claim on our economy's production, that is, more money to buy things they could not earlier afford. Rather, indexing merely enables pensioners to maintain, roughly, their same standard of living.
I think this states very clearly the attitude that the Prime Minister had when he wrote that letter and made that commitment, but now we find a complete reversal of ethics. It is hard to believe that the Prime Minister, the leader of this nation, would promote or subscribe to a policy that we are facing at the present time where that very principle has been eroded and destroyed by the introduction of this measure.
This is but one of three Bills which have been brought before this House and have occupied a considerable amount of time. The one presently before us deals with public employees, the second one with Family Allowances, and the third with Old Age Security. In presenting these Bills the Government is not claiming-or I do not think they are-that this legislation is going to have a great monetary effect on their financing of Government operations, but it is apparently its idea of equalizing participation in an economic recovery program. Rather than equalize it, it does just the opposite. To some it may have slight consequences, but to those to whom we are making reference today, it could mean a reduction in their income and in their ability to face the future in their retirement years. As far as those in the other parts of the six and five program are concerned, it means they are not able to meet the challenges facing them at this present time.

STATEMENTS PURSUANT TO S.O. 21
subsubtopic: WARNING AGAINST USE OF ASA IN TREATMENT OF CHILDREN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, ASA, acetylsalicylic acid, is the active ingredient of Aspirin and many other products taken for headaches and colds. A series of American studies have suggested that, for children with flu and chicken pox, the use of ASA can lead to a rare and often fatal brain disease called Reye's Syndrome.
In the United States, in one group of children with Reye's syndrome, 97 per cent had been given ASA when they had flu or chicken pox. In another group of children who had the same illnesses but did not develop Reye's Syndrome, only 61 per cent had taken ASA.
In the United States official public health warnings on stickers for ASA products are already in place which state:
Do not give this product to children under the age of 18 with chicken pox or flu. It contains an ingredient associated with Reye's Syndrome-an often fatal disease.
In Canada the responsibility for this kind of thing lies with the Department of National Health and Welfare. Although this Department sent a warning about ASA to doctors, there were no public warnings. There has not been a formal and systematic way of informing the vast majority of Canadians. It is unfortunate that, with the flu season already under way, no such warnings are yet in place. It is my hope and expectation that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) will make this a priority issue as soon as possible.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE
subsubtopic: DENIAL OF BENEFITS TO ADOPTIVE PARENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Unemployment Insurance Act provides for payments to a woman giving birth to a child, and properly so. But the same Act denies any payment to a woman who adopts a child. Most, if not all, provincial Governments require a woman who adopts a baby to remain in her home with the child for a period of six months. In other words, a working woman must leave her job for six months in order to adopt a child. Under the Act, UIC officials reject such claims, which otherwise qualify, on the basis that the mother is not available for work, or is not looking for a job.
A woman who adopts a child is a mother in every respect except that of giving birth to the child. She gives the child a name; she gives the child love and kindness; she gives the child a hope for the future. The task force report on unemployment in the 1980s recommended that the special conditions surrounding the payment of maternity benefits be removed, and that those benefits be extended to adoptive parents. The Human Rights Commission also supports such action. Canada owes much to the hundreds of parents who are adopting babies and children, rearing them in homes filled with love and understanding, and making them happy and useful citizens. The present law is discriminatory and unfair and should be changed now, giving adoptive parents the same rights accorded to natural parents.

speakerposition: Minister of Communications
subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS
subsubtopic: PORNOGRAPHIC PROGRAMMING ADVERTISED BY FIRST CHOICE PAY TV
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I indicated my position quite clearly yesterday in response to the question put to me by the Hon. Member for Trinity. It is quite clear that the licence issued to First Choice, and the licences issued to other Pay TV operators in Canada, contain conditions which are appended to them. It is quite clear also that if any one of these channels had applied for a pornographic Pay TV licence, that licence would have been refused by the CRTC, and certainly would have been refused on appeal to the Governor in Council.
It is not our intention to launch, with Pay TV, a pornographic film industry in Canada. It is our intention to see to it that Pay TV helps the Canadian program production industry to develop world-class programming.
As far as content is concerned, the Hon. Member knows that Parliament in its wisdom has given authority over content to the CRTC and that the CRTC has the necessary powers to examine the whole question. As I indicated yesterday in

First Choice has been advertising itself as "The Playboy Channel" and promises to show "the most adult of adult entertainment... TV like you've never seen before. Sizzling entertainment . . .And that's the bare truth."
Madam Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister whether, in his view, this is consistent with the Broadcasting Act. May I also remind him that it is not necessary to repeat the Broadcasting Act in the condition of licence. It is assumed that the station, network or whatever, will abide by the Broadcasting Act.

Madam Speaker, once again the Hon. Member has asked me to say whether I am in favour of the development of a pornographic industry in Canada. I have already indicated quite clearly that pornography has no place on Pay TV or on regular broadcasting stations in Canada. The laws of the land are already in place. Parliament in its wisdom has given the courts jurisdiction over the definition of obscenity and pornography and has not given that discretion to the Minister of Communications. Parliament has also given the necessary powers to the CRTC to monitor the situation and to take corrective action.
If the Hon. Member is asking me whether I have confidence in the Chairman of the CRTC and in the CRTC itself, the answer is yes.

In its conditions of licence and in the over-all powers given to it under the Broadcasting Act, the CRTC has all the powers necessary to enforce this.
What the Hon. Member is asking me to do is to intervene personally. Obviously the second question then is whether it is the job of the Government to intervene in such cases, or if Parliament was correct in saying that questions of content should be debated and handled in front of an independent organization such as the CRTC, all powers in this matter having been given to the CRTC by Parliament.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 wish to say a few words on the amendment before Bill C-133 is discussed this afternoon. I wish to make it clear that I wish to oppose the amendment. I think it is very unfair and very unjust.
First of all, it is an amendment to increase the 6 per cent raise in this particular legislation to 6.5 per cent, a measly one half of 1 per cent. That shows the generosity of the Liberal Party of Canada across the way.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext: It is $18 million.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
It may be $18 million, but the Liberal Party across the way gives many more millions to big companies and to all kinds of people through very extensive tax write-offs.
As a matter of fact, I could not help but note in the statement made by the Bishops of Canada on January 5 that the top 20 per cent of the Canadian people make 42 per cent of Canada's national income and the bottom 20 per cent make 4 per cent of Canada's national income. What the Bishops are saying, and I want to quote them, is that we need more balance and that an equitable program should be developed for reducing and stemming the tide of inflation. This would require shifting the burden for wage controls to the upper income earners and introducing controls on prices and new forms of taxes on investment income such as dividends and interest. I think that is the crux of the whole six and five debate which is before the House.
I do not think anyone argues that we do not need a restraint program; most countries in the world do have restraint programs. But the whole problem is, who is going to pay the price? Who is going to pay the price to bring down inflation in this country? The Government decided it will be the ordinary worker, the pensioner, the kids of this nation. Ordinary people will have to pay the price of inflation in Canada.
For example, a 6 per cent increase for someone with an income of $10,000 will result in an additional $600. However, for someone with an income of $50,000, a 6 per cent increase will result in an additional $3,000. What kind of fairness is that when the poor guy gets an increase of $600 and the wealthy person receives an increase of $3,000 a year? All that
January 18, 1983

does is add to the disparities, the unfairness and inequities in this country for the top 20 per cent who earn 42 per cent of the national income and the bottom 20 per cent who earn 4 per cent of the national income.
I suggest this legislation should provide the converse. Everything we do in this country should be directed toward narrowing the gap between the rich and the poor. I recommend that all Members read the statement by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops issued on January 5. In many places they speak about the moral obligation of politicians, the business community and others in this country to help the poor and the ordinary working people of Canada. They say, and I quote:
The first principle has to do with the preferential option for the poor, the afflicted, and the oppressed. In the tradition of the Prophets, Jesus dedicated his ministry to bringing "good news to the poor" and "liberty to the oppressed". As Christians, we are called to follow Jesus by identifying with the victims of injustice, by analyzing the dominant attitudes and structures that cause human suffering, and by actively supporting the poor and oppressed in their struggles to transform society.
Bill C-133 does not do what the Bishops of Canada suggest, identifying with the poor and those less done by. Instead, the Bill before this House will make the poor and the ordinary worker pay more. In this case the retired public servant will pay more while the wealthy in this country pay less as they get more and more tax breaks from the Government supported, unfortunately, by the Progressive Conservatives in this House of Commons.
I repeat, this statement should be required reading for all Members of Parliament. In their statement the Bishops make reference to the kind of economic programs we should have in this country. They say it is not moral that we have 1.5 million jobless in this country. I recommend this document to each and every Member.
I hope that the Liberal backbenchers, many of whom I believe are sincere, will be able to persuade their colleagues in Cabinet who are isolated from the real facts not to fight inflation on the backs of the ordinary people, the poor, the oppressed and the unemployed, but rather that we fight inflation by restricting the incomes of the very wealthy or clamping down on excessive prices and profits and the many tax loopholes that there are for the wealthy and the coupon clippers of this country. We should not fight inflation on the backs of the poor and the pensioners in Canada. The right way is to deal with those who can afford it. That is not only the best way economically but the moral way to get out of this crisis.
If the Bill before us stated that the incomes of the lowest paid Canadians would be increased by the cost of living plus 3, 4, 15 or 18 per cent, or something like that, that those with incomes of $50,000 and more, such as Members of Parliament, would receive an increase of 2 or 3 per cent or no increase, and that those making higher incomes would have their salaries rolled back, I would agree with an inflation program and a restraint program. However, I do not agree with an inflation program that tightens the belt of the skinniest person so much that he cannot breathe and gives the overweight person extra elastic in his pants so that he can expand indefinitely as he enjoys life and the fat of the land.
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
That is not fair. It is not the direction we should be taking in our country. Nor is it the vision we should have for Canadians. In fact, in addition to giving working Canadians and other ordinary Canadians more of the national income, they should be given more of a say, more power and more rights in the workplace. Workers in the communities and farmers should own more and more of our economy. However, there are those in this House, particularly in the extreme right in the Progressive Conservative Party, who complain about the present day Petro-Canada, CBC and other public ownership. That is the direction we should be going.
I am sorry, I cannot hear the interjection of the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone). I suggest that he study the statement of the Bishops. He will find that they refer to alternative economic approaches that we should be taking in this country. I quote from page 6:
There are, of course, alternative ways of looking at our industrial future and organizing our economy. This does not imply a halt to technological progress but rather a fundamental re-ordering of the basic values and priorities of economic development. An alternative economic vision for example, could place priority on serving the basic needs of all people in this country, on the value of human labour, and an equitable distribution of wealth and power among people and regions. What would it mean to develop an alternative economic model that would place emphasis on-socially-useful forms of production; labour-intensive industries; the use of appropriate forms of technology; self-reliant models of economic development; community ownership and control of industries; new forms of worker management and ownership; and greater use of the renewable energy sources in industrial production?
That is exactly the opposite of what we hear from many Members on both sides of the House. They say we have too little of society oriented toward profit-making, stock markets, private investment, and that there are not enough write-offs for dividends, investments and tax credits. That is the opposite of what the Bishops recommend.
1 hope this document of the Bishops will become an historic turn-around in this country toward a society that is more moral, just and equal for each and every Canadian and each and every region. If the Bishops succeed in doing that, they have made a contribution to Canada that is much greater, I am sad to say, than the national Parliament of Canada is making through the words uttered in this House.
I believe I have another minute or two, but I see you getting edgy, Mr. Speaker.
