Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak in opposition to the amendment proposed by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) as well as the provisions of this Bill. When one looks at the amendment advanced by the President of the Treasury Board, one readily sees that it is a measly admission of the fact that this Government's approach is wrong. If it had the courage, it would withdraw not only the amendment but the legislation. If it had any confidence in its six and five program, this kind of legislation would not be necessary.
I am surprised in listening to the debate that the NDP seem to focus the bulk of their words on an attack against the

January 18, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
Conservative Party. They are more inclined to attack the Conservative Party, who are not the authors of this piece of legislation, rather than attack the Liberal Government, which is the author of these provisions. More and more Canadians are coming to the realization that the Liberal-NDP socialist alliance that has governed this country over the last 15 years is certainly not working. It is the NDP which kept this Government in office during the period from 1972 to 1974. It is the NDP which triggered this Government's return to power, but now they stand around and indirectly criticize the Liberal Government, but they are more inclined to attack the Progressive Conservative Party which obviously has a greater share of political support in Canada than perhaps the Liberals and NDP combined. So they are basically fighting for their political survival.
I hearken back, Mr. Speaker, to lectures we received from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) this fall when he emphasized the necessity for trust and the need for Canadians in all corners of Canada to pull together. I have listened to this debate and there have been some very impassioned pleas and sincere appeals from Members on this side, asking the Government to reconsider this legislation. The Liberals are asking Members to put their country first. They are asking senior citizens and other groups, those unorganized and unable to fend for themselves, to bear the brunt of the six and five program. The Liberals are breaking a promise and commitment, once again employing that double standard which has been the hallmark of this Government. The Government has one law for its friends and one law for other people. It does not ask the Pitfields or the people who have been the recipients of the huge bail-outs to restrain or cut back. Rather, it calls upon that group in society which has the most difficulty fending for itself.
The Government points out that it needs the revenue. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is inaccurate and clearly misleading because this Government has always found money to buy service stations and nationalize oil companies. Look at what the Government has spent through PetroCan. It gobbled up Pacific Petroleum for $1.5 billion; Atlantic Richfield for $342 million; Petrofina for $1.4 billion, and then the latest acquisition of a string of service stations for $600 million. That is $4 billion in the last two years. The Government found money to spend on those kinds of enterprises, but we have to ask ourselves whether that expenditure has really been in the best interests of Canada. I have before me an assessment of Petro-Can's competitive potential related to its low-cost capital structure as outlined by Ultramar Canada, and I want to quote from a document they presented. They say:
Pctro-Canada obtained its equity capital 'free' from the Federal Government and pays little interest on its debt.
It reported retained earnings of $176 million on December 31, 1981 after six years of operations. If Petro-Canada during those years had been obliged to find its capital, and reward its shareholders and lenders on the same terms as a private sector integrated oil company, subject to the rigorous discipline of
financial markets and commercial reality, it would have reported a cumulative deficit in the order of $341 million.
This is a variance of $517 million, financed by taxpayers and consumers in ways few of them understand, and potentially enabling Petro-Canada to wield irresistible power in the market place.
There you have it, Mr. Speaker. The Government has money for that sort of enterprise which is really, according to this assessment, not a very good investment. It has not even paid simple interest in terms of return on investment. We also know this Government is extracting billions and billions of dollars from the western provinces and resource industries. I have a recap of the cumulative total which this Government has extracted in the field of energy related taxes and it works out to about $11 billion over an 18 month period. It is now working out to a rate of about $7 billion or $8 billion a year in taxes extracted from the consumer and taxpayer as the result of this Government's imposition of its energy tax program. So when we talk about money, it is simply a matter of the allocation of funds and priorities, and this Government has chosen, as a priority, to spend money buying service stations rather than providing for protection to retired civil servants and the people of Canada with young families who are finding it very difficult to cope in this very depressed economic state.
When we speak of trust, Mr. Speaker, we simply have to refresh our memory about what this Government said during the last election campaign and the 1974 election campaign. We all know the issue was wage and price controls. We know the Government, particularly the Prime Minister, was very critical of a policy outlined by our Party in support of a freeze and a regime of wage and price controls. He promised the Canadian people that would never occur. Well, we know what happened, that is history. We also know that in the 1980 campaign there were some rather irresponsible promises made by this Prime Minister and his Government, amongst which was this, and I quote from The Toronto Star of January 26, 1980:
Trudeau: "We will enhance the security of the individual through measures such as the increase in the guaranteed income supplement which helps one of the groups in our society-the elderly poor-that needs help most.
I could go on and quote the promises regarding cheap energy, or talk about the security of individuals and what the Government was going to do with respect to the problems of unemployment. Just a short quotation would certainly be most revealing at this particular time. At the University of Saskatchewan on January 16, 1980, Mr. Trudeau stated this:
On jobs, we will not increase unemployment by 100,000 jobs this year as the Tories promised to do in their budget.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on behalf of my constituents in Burnaby on Bill C-133, and in particular on the amendment which is before the House. It is basically an attempt to buy off Liberal backbenchers who had expressed a certain amount of opposition to the Bill in its original form.
The amendment would increase the annual rate of indexation by one half of one percent in 1983 and in 1984. What this means is that those Liberal backbenchers who have changed their minds and have now agreed to support the measure- which is an invidious attack on the standard of living of thousands of elderly people in Canada-have been bought for a price of approximately ten cents per day. That is the amount of the increase the amendment would bring to the average pension of the people affected by the Bill.
The Bill constitutes a direct attack on the standard of living of thousands of my constituents in Burnaby-retired members of the Public Service, retired members of the Armed Services and retired members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The Government has broken faith with close to 200,000 retired federal employees. The breakdown for 1980-81 showed some
120,000	retired members of the Public Service, 32,000 retired members of the Canadian Armed Force, 2,200 retired members of the RCMP and other retirees, bringing the total to about 160,000 people. This figure will be increased over the next two years to about 200,000 people.
We are talking about individual retired federal employees who, over the course of their employment, contributed 1 per cent of their salary to a special supplementary retirement benefits fund for the purpose of protecting the purchasing
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
power of their pensions. In addition, they contributed 6.5 per cent of their salary each year for their basic pensions.
1 want to emphasize that what the Government is doing is breaking a sanctified contract with public servants who, in good faith, contributed deferred wages, in effect, amounting to 1 per cent of their salary, for the purpose of protecting the purchasing power of their pensions against an increase in the cost of living. The Government has made use of those funds contributed by retired federal employees, for its own purposes and has not invested them to bring the best possible return. Once again, the retired federal employees are contributing in that way to the good of the country, only to have the Government stab them in the back through the means of Bill C-133.
We are not talking about wealthy individuals, Mr. Speaker. The average pensioner affected by the Bill has a pension of $6,900 per year. Many of them are survivors and 83 per cent of survivors receive a pension of less than $5,500 per year. Most of the survivors are elderly women struggling to get along on incomes well below the poverty line.
The effect of this iniquitous Bill is to rob retired federal employees of over $100 million over a two-year period. For the average pensioner that means a loss in 1983 of some $345 or, for the two years, some $1,200. At the same time, the Government is eroding the base of these pensions for future years. This is a Government that talks about equity, that asks pensioners to contribute on a fair and equitable basis to the fight against inflation. It asks pensioners, in effect, to take a cut in their real standard of living.
What equity exists in a Government which, at the same time as it slashes the standard of living of federal retired employees, cuts the marginal tax rate of the highest income earners in the country? What equity exists in a Government which, at the same time as it cuts the standard of living of elderly retired public employees, allows some 4,850 Canadians who earned more than $50,000 in 1980 to pay not a penny in income tax? This fact is revealed in the most recent taxation statistics for this country. In that same year, 179 taxpayers who earned over $200,000 paid not one penny in income tax as well.
The Government should hang its head in shame for asking retired federal employees to take a cut in their real standard of living at the same time as it allows the wealthiest in our society to escape paying any income tax whatsoever. At the same time, it has introduced legislation which would cut by 10 per cent the marginal tax rate of the wealthiest people in the country, those most able to shoulder the burden of the fight against inflation. The Government certainly does not in any way display the principles of equity and justice which should be displayed in the circumstances.
Bill C-133, Bill C-131 which deals with old age pensions, and Bill C-132 which deals with Family Allowances flow directly from the six and five legislation which the Progressive Conservative Party overwhelmingly supported in June 1982. In the documents which accompanied that legislation it was explicitly stated that at the heart of the six and five proposals was a cut in the standard of living, not just of federal public

Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
servants but of retired federal employees, including retired members of the RCMP, the Canadian Forces and others.
The Conservative Party was fully aware of the consequences of six and five, yet it voted with the Liberals 16 times, in recorded votes, to support the legislation which is resulting in a cut in the standard of living of over 200,000 elderly people in the country. What hypocrisy, Mr. Speaker.

I could not put this matter any better than it has been put by many of my constituents in correspondence with me. I should like to quote from a letter sent by a Mrs. McIntosh of Wildwood Avenue, Burnaby, which is one of many I have received. She writes:
I am writing this letter to protest the proposed government legislation to limit the indexing of civil service pensions to 6 per cent. I can understand the need for restraint in these trying times, but it should not be at the expense of something that we have already paid for. During our working years, civil servants were told that in return for a percentage of their wages, they would receive a pension fully indexed to the cost of living increase for that year. If a private individual tried a stunt like that they would probably land in jail for fraud.
How true that is, Mr. Speaker.
In 1977, in response to correspondence on the question of the indexing of Public Service pensions, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had this to say:
Pensioners are out of the work force and cannot bargain or strike for larger incomes. They are not the cause of inflation; they are its victim. We have an obligation to help protect them.
I note in passing that they are the victims of the economic policies for which the Liberal Government is responsible. The Liberals have been in power for almost all of the last 15 or 20 years in this country, with a brief interregnum.
I know my time is coming to an end. I would like to close by emphasizing the fact that Bill C-133 and the proposed amendment to buy a few votes on the Liberal side constitute nothing less than an assault on the standards of living of some of the people in the country who are the least able to afford the burden. I have heard from many of my constituents. 1 have heard from Mr. Glen Scott, President of the South Burnaby branch of the Royal Canadian Legion, and from hundreds of others who insist that the Government should respect the commitments it made to them and to the people of the country and withdraw this odious piece of legislation.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to make some brief comments on this infamous Bill and the rather stupid amendment to Bill C-133, to cap the retirement benefits of public servants. Actually it is a Bill which gives the Government a licence to steal. Heaven only knows that the
people of Canada have lost enough faith already in the Government. To bring in a piece of legislation like this breaks a legal contract without any prior consultation with a group of people who can least fight for themselves in the struggle to keep their heads above water during retirement years.
We in the NDP are outraged because if a trade union broke a legal contract I am quite convinced that the Government members, and certainly the Conservatives, would be up on their feet yelling and screaming all afternoon, day after day. Let us not forget that the Conservatives supported the Government with Bill C-124 which brought in the whole six and five program. We in the NDP were the only Party in Ottawa to oppose it. Now it is easy to understand why one Tory after another is rising to try to heal his or her conscience. They are trying to get across the idea that that is not what they had in mind when they supported Bill C-124, that they did not anticipate that it would be extended to include retired public servants. Nonetheless, they supported the six and five program at that time because they felt that the majority of Canadians were for it. Perhaps that is true, if one wants to be led by the polls like sheep, but one must have the courage to face reality afterwards. Apparently that is not being done in this debate by the Conservative Opposition.
There are a few facts with respect to Bill C-133 that 1 would like to put on the record. I hope they will clear up some misconceptions and misinterpretations as far as the general public is concerned. To begin with, the Bill really amounts to the theft of $165 million from an account paid into and contributed to by public servants during their working years, based upon a 1 per cent additional payment by them as a hedge against inflation during retirement years; in other words, the indexing of pensions. Public employees pay 7.5 per cent of their salary to support the pension plan. On the other hand, in the private sector employee contributions seldom exceed 5 per cent and are frequently less. This is something which is not generally known by the public, that Public Service employees actually contribute more to their pension plan than do most employees in the private sector-7.5 per cent of their salary to support their pension plan.
1 have another series of figures which 1 should like to put on the record. The benefits paid from the plan to date have been more heavily financed by employees than by their employer. Of $1,360 million paid out between October 1981 and September 1982, employees contributed $735 million compared with the Government's $625 million. Here again this is usually not the case in the private sector. Usually in the private sector it is the employer who pays the larger share and, in some cases as a result of agreement, the employer pays all of the contribution to the pension plan. During their contributing years federal public servants pay more than the private sector at 7.5 per cent, and in contributions back they have actually paid more for the contributions than their employer.
Another fact I should like to put on the record is that currently there is a surplus of $15.5 billion in the Public Service Superannuation Account. The interest which can be earned on this amount is more than sufficient to pay for
January 18, 1983

indexation. The fund itself is in healthy shape. At this time it is not costing taxpayers one cent, yet the Government insists on cutting back the normal increase public servants would receive based on the cost of living. This was why they contributed the extra 1 per cent during their working years-as a hedge against inflation.
Previously the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) committed the Government to full indexation of Public Service pensions as a right earned during working years. I believe this was stated by the Prime Minister back in 1977. His Ministers previously defended the plan and argued that the Government could not break its contract with Public Service pensioners by reducing indexation. We must keep in mind that we are not dealing with only Clerks of the Privy Council or Deputy Ministers who retired on very handsome superannuation benefits because they were making very high incomes during their last five or six years of employment. We are dealing with literally thousands upon thousands of retired RCMP officers, retired military personnel and retired public servants who never got into the high income brackets during their working years. Like all retirees, they have no clout or strength in numbers to fight the Government. 1 argue very strongly that they were not the cause of inflation.
Ordinary Canadians, whether they be retired public servants or retirees from the private sector, did not have control over the economy. They did not make major decisions at the top which contributed to inflation, yet they are the ones who are expected to fight inflation by taking a reduced retirement pension when, even at the present time, well over half the
100,000	federal Public Service retirees can barely make ends meet, primarily as a result of the high inflation rate.
The Government's Green Paper on pension reform clearly supports the need to protect all pensions against the erosion of inflation. Many observers in the private sector agree with this.
I cannot think of anything more humane which a Government can do, at the federal or provincial level, than to guarantee its former employees who are now retired a secure and financially safe retirement. In most cases they have given the best years of their lives to the Government and its Public Service, yet now they are being kicked in the pants because of the Government s stupid financial policies which have brought about runaway inflation.
1 should like to close by simply stating that we in the NDP are unalterably opposed to Bill C-133. It is unfair, it is morally reprehensible, and it is a theft of some $165 million from contributions by public servants to their retirement fund as a hedge against inflation. It is an odious Bill. It should be withdrawn, and the amendment to raise the increase from 6 per cent to 6.5 per cent and from 5 per cent to 5.5 per cent is nothing short of a sick joke.

This amendment is ludicrous. Just listen to the baying hounds to my left, the cohorts of the people across the way.
This amendment, amounting to a half of one per cent, is an admission by the Government of a disastrous Bill, of an inequitable Bill. It is adding to the confidence crisis in this Government. It is a plague unto the savers of Canada who, by prepayment of their pensions-hundreds of thousands of them in the Armed Forces, the civil service and the RCMP- provided for their future now, only to find their future crim-bling like a sand castle by the actions of the highest court in the land, this Parliament that can change its mind. The underlying issue, as everyone is aware, is the credibility and accountability of this Government or, more correctly, the lack of it.
By introducing Bill C-133, the Government is once again going back on its word, just like the 18-cent a gallon tax. By doing so, this Government is proving that honesty and integrity, the things on which the Conservative Party is built, are words that this Government cannot comprehend in either official language.
This Government, having entered into a contract, a sacred contract, now seeks to break that contract. That provision was not in Bill C-124. This Government seeks to break that contract with little or no regard for the serious consequences to befall those with whom it contracted, and with little or no regard for the morality involved. That is the problem in Canada today.
It has been pointed out by many other speakers that for many years public employees paid 7.5 per cent of their salaries to support a pension fund. In that, of course, was a 1 per cent provision for indexation. The Government has chosen to ignore that.
In my firm we have a 5 per cent pension plan. Contributions of 5 per cent come from the employee and a like amount from management. Right now that fund draws 9.5 per cent. Those employees are secure. As their salaries increase, so does the

amount in the pension plan. As we refinance those moneys with increased interest payments, people are totally protected. Why then did this Government not put the principles of free enterprise into play? 1 will tell you why. It is because this Government supports the principles of the people to my left. This Government does not care. What does it do with the money? Is it actuarially sound? Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, what would happen if that money, that $15.5 billion surplus alone, not to mention all the rest of the money that was invested over those years, had been placed with a private insurance company with a letter of comfort, the backing of the Canadian Government? To have done that would have made sense. Had that money been invested through free enterprise there would be no need for me to stand here today talking about indexing of pensions, because the Government would have had money to burn had the money been in separate funds. But these people will laugh at Mr. Lougheed and his Heritage Fund. His Government places money at the disposal of people, where it belongs.

Even forgoing what 1 have just said, whether or not the notion of indexing was appropriate is not the issue here. The issue is the fact that public servants, Armed Forces personnel, RCMP personnel, contracted with their Government for the indexing of their pensions. They paid for it. They did that in good faith, but what happened? The Government can change the law at will in order to force its will upon the savers of Canada, many of whom are very low income earners, such as the private in the Army and the Government clerk who have put their years in for the service of Canada.
I would remind the Government that a contract is supposed to have legal status. There are laws in place to protect either party in a contract, and the Government's duty is to enforce those laws, not break them. Yet this Government wishes to enact a new law which will enable it to break a contract while destroying the confidence of the Canadian people. What is next? The Government is demonstrating once again that when a certain law does not suit its purpose it will bring in another law which will, no matter if it is through three budgets or by other means.
Surely, if the Government no longer supports the principle of indexing pensions for its employees, it should have the simple decency to honour its present obligations under the contract and change its rules for future employees. Certainly it is a dishonourable and discreditable act to tell a group of people that they will be assured of something through a contract and then be denied that assurance.
This Government's pension plan has been bogus from the beginning. It is not actuarially sound. Reports are made to give people the impression that they have a separate pension fund when, in reality, this money goes into the general revenue. Let me point out a few examples of what the Government does with this money, even with a $15.5 billion surplus. As was
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
pointed out by the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski) a few moments ago, its priorities are mixed up. It purchases oil companies for $4 billion, some of which is double the price of the stock, and the money leaves the country. In this area it has a $341 million deficit.
Let us review some of the loan transactions this Government has made. For example, there is a loan to China for approximately $49 million. The Auditor General's Report stated, "An interest-free loan to China was authorized under the Exports Credit Insurance Act interest-free." The Government is then willing to give a paltry .5 per cent to the people who have devoted their lives to the service of this country. I could cite many other examples of loans which have been made by this Government interest-free. There is an example of a loan which has a 35 year maturity, a five-year grace period and is interest free. It matures at various dates between April 2001 and November 2005 in the amount of $3.82 million. There is another loan for $18 million with a 20 year maturity and a five-year grace at 5 per cent. There is a myriad of these examples. It represents absolutely profligate spending and mismanagement. One only needs to consider countries such as Haiti and Jamaica for further examples.
Canadians realize what this Government is doing. The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) was the Member who pointed out the fact of that $15.5 million surplus. He made one of the best speeches last night of any I have heard in the House since I have been here. He pointed out the fallacious actions of this Government.
My hon. colleague, the Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) received a letter from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dated October 12, 1977. I would like to quote it again for the record. The Prime Minister said:
Pensioners are out of the workforce and cannot bargain or strike for larger incomes. They are not the cause of inflation. They are its victim. We have an obligation to protect them.
We see the Government's obligation through a law which says that its former obligation does not count. The Government cannot be believed. It will break a contract whenever it wishes.
The pension fund is not actuarially sound when it could be so very easily. The Government does not back free enterprise, and this country is going down that slippery slope to socialism every day that we stand in the House. It is into our pockets, into our lives, and we want it out. This cannot be done on the backs of pinchers.
Some Members opposite understand the principles that are involved in this issue. They have publicly indicated their opposition to this Bill. It is about time that they began to think. Member for Brant.
Having destroyed the Canadian economy, the Government is now crying poor and, in this instance as in others, is planning

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak to this Bill and to the amendment which is the half per cent solution presented by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray). It only penalizes civil servant pensioners more than the original six and five proposal.
Of course, 1 join my Party in strongly opposing Bill C-133 because it breaks a contract agreement with the civil servants.
It is a contract to ensure them full indexing on their pensions which they paid into with the intention of being protected from inflation. The Government is doubly penalizing Public Service retirees by arbitrarily imposing this six and five restraint on
them. It is destroying confidence in the credibility of the Government itself which already has very little credibility.
Over the years many civil servants have paid into their pensions while planning very carefully for their retirement. Some retire early in order to be protected from having to live on a limited income with high inflation.
Their employer, the Federal Government, agreed to full indexation and paid its share into these pension funds. The Government also made use of those funds to which the public servants had contributed from their salaries. It made use of these funds at a low interest rate for various projects, and it benefited more than fully from the money of its civil servants. We strongly oppose the fact that the Government now refuses to pay back the civil servants. Pensioners are unable to reduce their food intake by 6 per cent. They cannot depend on fuel costs being restrained to 6 per cent or that their rents will be held to an increase of 6 per cent.
Many pensioners in my riding are finding it very difficult to survive on their limited incomes, particularly if they are not living in their own homes. Civil service pensioners have worked hard for the federal Government and they will be doubly penalized by the Government, first, through Bill C-131, if passed, when there will be a cut-back on basic old age pension indexing to 6 per cent and 5 per cent. Then, of course, the Government wants to sock it to them again in this Bill which would impose 6.6 per cent, 6.5 per cent with the amendment, capping the cost of living indexing. Any way one looks at it, this is a terrible breach of confidence. It is really an immoral step that the Government is taking against its own employees, who work very hard for some of the people who are sitting in this House and voting for this Bill.
I would particularly like to concentrate on the plight of civil service pensioners who happen to be women. In the last couple of days we have heard much about gentleman's agreements in this country. I can tell Your Honour that those gentleman's agreements have not been too concerned with the actual prejudice on the part of the Government toward women employees in the Public Service. I would like to give several examples. We know that women clerks who went on strike to get equal pay had an agreement that their salaries would be increased, including a 12.25 per cent increase. However, under Bill C-124, their indexing was reduced to 6 per cent. When their union appealed to the President of the Treasury Board to exempt them under the clause that stated that any group can be exempted by the Governor-in-Council, he refused. This is the lowest paid group of public servants.
Then again, we consider many of the women who are working and struggling to try to improve their position in the Public Service. Of course, these women who are now pensioners worked at very low rates of pay. That is bad enough for those who are younger now and in the Public Service, but the ones who are retirees worked at unbelievably low rates of pay over the years. If we consider the number of women who have
January 18, 1983

a chance to get promotions in the Public Service, one finds a deplorable situation, once again. This is because the Government has no affirmative action program. There is the lack of kind of affirmative action program to which the Government gives lip service. We find, for example, that 63 per cent of women in Public Service earn under $18,000 while only 23 per cent of men earn under that amount. We also see that 78 per cent of women in the Public Service are in support categories, such as clerks and maintenance people, earning low wages, and only 22 per cent are in middle management or office positions. There has been very little improvement over the last few years, since the Government has given lip service to affirmative action. Now, of course, the Government is breaking a written contract with Public Service pensioners, particularly with these women who have worked for such low wages over the years and now receive low pensions. On top of that, they will be doubly cut by these two Bills concerning indexing. Any way one looks at it, this Bill must be withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to proceed with an example. To illustrate discrimination against women in the Public Service, and now against Public Service pensioners, I would like to refer to a woman to whom I spoke when I visited my riding last week. She was very concerned about this Bill. At that time she spoke about the male domination which still exists in the federal Government, even though there is supposedly equal treatment in Canada today. She said that women are working in the lowest paid jobs, they work for much shorter periods of time, and therefore they have lower pensions on the average.
In her particular case, she went back to work when she was 42 years old. She was the sole supporter of her family, with two young children. She worked as a typist for $192 a month in 1956 and slowly made her way up to a clerk-typist position and a little higher. Then she was forced by poor health to quit in 1960. She said that she is lucky because she has her own house and a little garden and can keep some of her costs down. This woman earns, from her superannuation from the federal Government, a mere $359 a month. That is very little for people to survive on in Vancouver.
I would like to say that not only do we object to the Bill because it is immoral, but also because of the fact that to the federal Government's employees it is a breach of faith on the part of the federal Government. It is extremely hard on federal Government pensioners who are the lowest paid people and who now face full inflation. They have no real protection against inflation. As I said, it is of major concern to this Party as it applies to women pensioners who were former civil servants in particular.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of my constituents in Vancouver-Kingsway to speak on this amendment to Bill C-133. As Your Honour knows, the Bill itself decreases the amount of civil service pensions next year and the subsequent year to a level of six and five, 6 per cent and 5 per cent, rather than the inflation rate which was the original bargain, and thereby decreases the amount of money which should legitimately come to retired civil servants. In other words, the war against inflation will be fought in part by the retired civil servants in Canada.
The amendment changes the Bill somewhat. It increases the annual rate of indexing by .5 per cent in 1983 and 1984. Therefore, with the amendment, it means that the increases will be 6.5 per cent and 5.5 per cent. The change, I am told, is to placate some Liberal Government backbenchers. How easily, sir, they are placated! Their support is literally bought for 10 cents a day. They are easily sold out.
I rise to speak on the Bill because it is an attack on some of my constituents in Vancouver-Kingsway, specifically, on retired civil servants, on retired Armed Forces personnel, on retired RCMP personnel and others. I am told that there are
200,000	people in this country, in Canada, who will be affected by the Bill. I know that there are a number of people, affected in my riding of Vancouver-Kingsway, because I have received letters, visits and telephone calls about this matter. I am told that 1 per cent of civil servants' salaries went into a special fund to protect the purchasing power of those salaries.
The Parliamentary Secretary raised the question as to whether there is a contract involved. I am told that the Government states that there is not a contract between itself and its employees in terms of pensions. The unions state that when the Government was preparing for collective bargaining, the unions approached the civil service associations in the 1960s to suggest that superannuation be excluded from collective bargaining. In return, they were promised that there would be no unilateral changes in the program. An advisory committee was established and, until the present time, the Government kept its promise about no changes without consultation.
I note that Bert Hill, in an article in the Ottawa Citizen on January 5, said that "This puts the Government in the same position as some backward private employers who see pensions as a privilege rather than a right earned during the working years".
There was an agreement, in a sense, and this agreement has really been broken. This is a Government which seems to be prepared to break agreements and bargains, and that is a dangerous trend, because I do not think that governments in Canada were like that in the past. The Government is prepared to break the Crow rate agreement with farmers. It is even prepared to break agreements with Parliament. Concerning the pre-build of the Alaska Pipeline, it did not even come back to consult this Parliament when it wanted to change a fundamental law of Parliament. It is prepared to break an agreement with employees across the country when it implements

January 18, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
the six and five program and it breaks collective agreements with the Public Service. I say that this is morally wrong.
1 have before me a recent statement of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops. The Bishops say that there has been a breakdown in the morality of Canada. All we have to do is to look at our own Government. I believe that moral priorities are linked with political decisions, as the Bishops have said in their report. I say, and I think many other people feel this way, that it is morally wrong for the Government to change this agreement that it has with their retired employees.
The other day the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni) said that it was up to the retired civil servants to fight the battle against inflation. In the first place, this is the wrong battle. We should be fighting against the problem of unemployment, not inflation. We have the wrong people fighting the wrong problem.
Dome Petroleum is offered $500 million to bail it out, along with the banks. There are petroleum incentive grants of $8.6 billion offered in this country to the oil companies. Maislin is bailed out; Chrysler is bailed out; any company can be bailed out. Even in British Columbia we have got to the point where we bail out a ski hill, Whistler's Mountain. Then we penalize and freeze the incomes of civil servants. What we have in this country is socialism for the rich. That is what we have achieved after all these years, I am loathe to say.
Is it not about time we asked the people who can best afford to bear the burden of this recession, as the Catholic Bishops have said in their report, to do so, instead of picking upon the poor civil servants and especially on retired Armed Forces personnel who cannot speak for themselves when they are in the Army and who are now speaking through their organization? It is simply not fair. It is simply immoral to pick on the Armed Forces retirees. They are the people who fought for this country, who served this country. We do not want them to have to fight further battles in their retirement. We want to help them in their retirement. I think this is where it is morally wrong.
Pensioners have written to me from my riding and from all across Canada. To illustrate, I just want to read a letter from Mr. H. R. Gillespie of Hoy Street in my riding. He says:
As a retired civil servant, I would like to protest the Bill C-133 as it applies to superannuation pensions. While employed I was required to contribute 6.5 per cent of my salary to the Superannuation Account and an additional I per cent to the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Account. The latter deduction was made to provide for pension indexing (as defined in section 2(1) of the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act). I support FULL indexing to be applied at the current rate of inflation as measured by StatsCan for the year 1982, on January 1, 1983.
The letter continues:
In all honesty, the Government does not have the right to use this money for purposes other than maintaining the pension funds. For them to have changed the rules of indexing when it was paid for by myself and all other civil servants, both retired and continuing workers, is completely unacceptable. I will monitor the performance of those Members in Parliament who can protest this injustice and influence my family accordingly, when next we have an election.
I can assure Mr. Gillespie that we in the New Democratic Party, and myself in particular from Vancouver-Kingsway, support him 100 per cent in the thoughts he has expressed in his letter.
I have had letters from other constituents. Pensioners' organizations and professional organizations have written to us. All of them, except perhaps for the superannuates' national organization the executive of which, in my view, badly represents its members, have been very supportive, and I quote from a letter from the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada dated January 14, 1983. It says in part:
The New Democratic Party has steadfastly supported public service pensioners, in their fight to defeat a bill which seeks to legitimize the theft of $165 million as part of the Government's political battle against inflation.
We are grateful for that support and we will continue to fight.
Before I sit down I would like to speak to two other matters.
I say this to the Conservative Party, and 1 have listened to some of their speeches. They should have realized, when they agreed to support the six and five program in principle, that bills like this would affect the old people, the children, and now the retired people from the Armed Forces and the Public Service. It is beneath contempt to make the argument about the NDP voting to increase our salaries. They know that is nonsense. The NDP voted against the six and five Bill, and the Conservatives should have voted against it in principle because the logical outcome is this particular Bill.
I want to conclude by saying this. I am ashamed for my country-and I say this to the Canadian people, if I might- that we are attacking the Public Service of Canada. If one were to go today to Fraser Street in my riding, to the UIC Office, one could see what it is like to be a clerk in that office, with a line-up of thousands of unemployed. So let us not attack them; we should be supporting them. We should be helping them in this dire time. That is fundamental justice. Instead, we seem to be morally bankrupt here in bringing in an amendment such as this and a Bill such as this in which we go after retired civil servants, the retired Armed Forces personnel and the retired RCMP personnel to make them bear the brunt of the war against inflation. All this, while we let the big, rich guys off. In my view, that is morally wrong.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the NDP. They tell us, as members for sanctimony, that somehow we are against the aged, the retired, that we in the Conservative Party, because we voted for a Bill, can take the least likely stance that they can paint and say we are for all of its follow up legislation. It is like asking us, "Why do you vote for the pizza you want, when you oppose anchovies?" The fact of the matter is, if they can paint the light, that somehow there is any Party in this House or any group of citizens anywhere in this country who opposes those who are retired from receiving a decent income, then it is every bit as legitimate for us to tell them that when they voted against Bill C-124 they voted against it because they were protecting their own salaries. In other words, as the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) just said, it was nonsense for us in the Conservative Party to tell the NDP that the only reason they voted against Bill C-124 is because they did not want their salaries to be cut. It is nonsense, but it is every bit as logical as their telling us or anyone else in this House that there are some people here who are opposed to retired people.
So, if I may set that question aside, I want to say that what we have here is pizza legislation. Parties will differ because there will be some parts they like and others they disagree with. It is not to say that the six and five program is wrong, or our Party is wrong in seeing that the six and five was brought in. What is wrong is that the application is selective, that is, it applies to a section of society, generally from welfare to average, but does not apply to those in the average to high income bracket. That is one of the principles that is wrong.
The other principle that is wrong is the question of breach of contract. Members opposite say there was no written contract. What a thin veil to hide behind, because we can still see right through. The truth of the matter is, whether it was written on paper or otherwise, the members of the civil service paid extra money for the purpose of receiving the extra pension.
If it was to be the view of Government, supported by Parliament, that there would be a time when public servants should not receive as high a pension, right or wrong, that could be accepted, but not after the contribution payments had already begun. Who in their right mind would believe that after having made payments for the purpose of receiving a higher income, along would come big government and say that it is sorry, "Although you have made the payments, you will not get a higher retirement income"?
Who on the Liberal side can rise and say there is no contract? Although it has collected $14 million more from the public servants in Canada in terms of payments, it now says there is no written contract. Whether it is written or not, there is a contract. There is an agreement whereby if public servants were to set aside more money, they would receive more in return.
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
Other Members have pointed out that what is wrong here is the question of the principle of allocation of Government priority. In other words, while they argue that in this time of restraint they can no longer pay for pensions, they can build airports that are massive and opulent and buy oil companies at double their value as well as introducing a Crown corporation that would destroy the right of enterprise in the marketplace of agricultural products.
In other words, what the Government is doing is simply reaching into the grab bag and picking on those groups their pollsters tell them they can pick on. The news media has widely circulated the fact that through polling Canadians, the Liberals have found out that public servants can be picked on politically. It is not a question of justice or the law of Parliament, but simply whom they can safely pick on politically. This is done on the basis that right across this country there are public servant jokes such as, "How does a public servant wink? He opens one eye". That is the view of the Government on the basis of polls, even though it knows it is wrong. It tells the people of Canada that because there is no contract, it can do as it wishes with public servants.
We talk about six and five and now the amendment to 6.5 and 5.5. That is very much like yelling to the person who is drowning not to worry because we have taken a pail of water out of the lake. If one's income is degenerating, having it degenerate by not quite so much is of very little comfort.
I want to share this perspective. Many Canadians who hear this debate will view it in the context of a public servant and think of him as having retired yesterday or today.

speechtext: Him or her.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
I am sorry, I stand corrected. Obviously I meant persons, people, him or her. I certainly want to give all the credit one can to that hard-working army of females in the Canadian Public Service who deserve the compliments of everyone in this House of Commons. The point is that Canadians generally think of them as having retired either presently or very recently. The truth is, and this was mentioned previously by others, some of the public servants retired a decade or more ago. They made their contribution to their pension benefits. Because of inflation in recent years, they are in a very desperate situation today. To limit them in the same way that would limit someone who has recently retired and has caught up with the present inflation rate is basically inexcusable. Those who retired in the sixties or early seventies as a result of the limits of this legislation will have their pensions cut in a way that will severely limit their buying power.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are giving me a signal to tell me my time is up. It certainly is not a signal to tell me that there is an end to the issue. We can talk for a long time on this.
We must remember there is a specific injustice. The Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) reminded me of this when I said "him" rather than "them". She is very right in talking about public servants to a large degree being female and that to a very significant extent females are in the lower income brackets. This legislation will apply more to them and

January 18, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
will cause even more discrimination with regard to their pensions.
We need to talk about the principle of this legislation. First, if there are going to be programs such as six and five, they must be universal throughout society. Second, you cannot breach a contract, which this Bill and this amendment does. Those two principles have been broken by the Government. For those reasons, we are fighting the Bill.
The NDP refer to how we voted before. We must restrain ourselves as a society. They now find individual warts in this legislation. That in no way deters us from the principle that we must practise restraint at a time of inflation. Flowever, the Progressive Conservatives are strongly opposed to the suggestion that (a) the Government has the right to select or (b) that it has the right to breach a contract. My time is up. There is much more we should talk about. 1 hope Members of the NDP recognize that if they continue to speak in opposition toward this Party which did not introduce the legislation, they simply implicate themselves as to whom they are afraid of at the time of the next election.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to speak today to the amendment to Bill C-133. It is an opportunity to express some of the views of my constituents who are concerned that their pensions are being eroded by the unilateral action of a federal Government which they thought had some commitment to pension reform. I will quote from a few letters I have received. It is important that we know whom we are talking about when we talk about the Public Service and those who are affected by the legislation. I quote:
For many years we paid the contribution required toward the full indexing and we were assured that our pensions would always be fully indexed.
That was written by a pensioner who served for four and a half years in the RCAF and 3016 years in the Public Service. I quote another pensioner as follows:
With times as they are now, 1 need all the pension I can get to keep up with today's prices and rates. The indexation was set and promised by the Government and 1 feel betrayed.
The individual who wrote that worked in the Post Office for 21 years. Another constituent wrote:
This is a contract entered into with the federal Government and should not be broken ... I say we have paid for this in advance.
Fie paid into the superannuation fund for 35 years. Finally, a fourth constituent wrote:
If any company or corporation had handled pension funds in this manner, they would be jailed or out of business or both ... 1 trust your Party will take a strong stand against this proposed Government measure.
We in the NDP have demonstrated, not only on Bill C-133 but on Bills C-132 and 131, that we are not prepared to see the standard of living of our pensioners and our children eroded by legislation that will not generate any economic activity in this country but will simply lead to greater and greater recession.
I might say to the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), who has obviously been keeping an eye on the number
of speakers in this debate, that we have now had 18 Conservative Members and 1 am the fifteenth Member of the NDP to speak. 1 would like to remind the Hon. Member that we were expecting there would be the normal three Conservative Members speaking against this legislation for every New Democrat, and we will be anxious to tally up at the end of the debate on this amendment just what the outcome is. I certainly will be interested in hearing what comments the Conservatives have to offer.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I regret very much that I made an error when I said we had 17 speakers. We actually had 19, and now we have had 20 compared to the NDP 14, and now 15.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
I see the Conservatives still have some difficulty counting, Mr. Speaker.
We are opposing this legislation because we have pensioners in our ridings who thought they had some security. As we all know, the superannuants have paid 6.5 per cent of their wage into a pension fund, but beyond that they have contributed 1 per cent of their income to a supplementary retirement benefit account. That was specifically to protect them against the erosion of inflation. They were probably in an enviable position, considering what the rest of the pension system in Canada is like, to be able to do that. They considered that contribution as a deferred wage, and the former President of the Treasury Board recognized that.
The Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) indicated there is some sensitivity in the public about public servant's salaries and pensions. We seem to have in Canada a group of individuals who do not particularly like to see public pension plans or government involvement in those plans. We have seen the spectre of exorbitant pensions being paid to retired public servants and Members of Parliament. If those indexed pensions were extrapolated over 20 years at about a 10 per cent inflation rate, certainly they would be immense. But what we are dealing with here is an average pension of about $8,100 a year. If we look at the widows' and survivors' benefits of those public pensions, they are even worse. One figure I have read is $3,200, but if 1 look at the Superannuants Association figures, they estimate a typical surviving spouse as a meagre pension of about $2,000, which will be reduced under this legislation to about $1,800. That is a pretty pitiful amount of money for a surviving spouse to have from a pension fund into which the employees paid 7.5 per cent of their wages. We are dealing with a tax on retired public servants which is going to cost them on average about $1,200 over the next two years, for a total saving of $100 million or $150 million to the Government. Because that money would normally have been used to generate further economic activity, it will help to depress the economy. The Government has recently published a Green Paper on pensions called "Better Pensions for Canadians". It lists some of the serious failings of our pension system as follows:
Some elderly people who are single, particularly single women, have incomes that are insufficient.
January 18, 1983

Inflation has eroded the value of employer-sponsored pensions for many Canadians who are now retired and has also eroded the value of benefits accumulated by employees who are still at work.
Many employees will ultimately receive little pension income, even after many years of work, because they do not stay in one job long enough to acquire vested benefits.
Even if vested benefits are acquired, pensions are generally not "portable" when an employee changes jobs.
A significant number of working people are likely to experience declines in their living standards when they retire, in large measure because employer-sponsored pension plans are not universally available, because they lack sufficient opportunity to accumulate retirement savings, or because pension plan benefits are not sufficiently large.
Elere we have Government employees who were at least some way down the road to improving pensions, but we now have a Government which arbitrarily degrades the only bright spot in the pension scheme in Canada, probably to the benefit of private pension plans. What is going to happen ultimately, when old age pensioners and superannuates see the attitude of the Government to pensioners? In order to protect their retirement income they will have to turn more to private industry. I would challenge the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to use some of her clout within cabinet to see that legislation of this nature is withdrawn, and withdrawn immediately.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to examine this amendment in slightly more detail than we have been doing so far, let me say that it is really a problem in the sense that it is an insult to Parliament and the senior citizens and civil servants who have served this country for so long. Today we find a Government which wants to steal money from those people, money they have paid over the years, 6.5 per cent for a pension plan, followed by 1 per cent for indexation. Now the Government would literally steal from those who have paid into that fund. The proposal put forward by the Government is that the thief return part of his ill-gotten gains, and a very paltry amount at that. That is clearly an insult and the House should be offended, as should civil servants who depend on that indexed pension.
There is no doubt that the amendment offers a number of courses of action, and perhaps it would be useful to list them for my Conservative colleagues. The Government is absolutely intransigent on this particular point and has no intention of backing off. No matter how foul the proposed legislation, the Government will go through with it. It is a matter of saving face. However, it might be useful to outline the problem for our colleagues who share the Opposition benches.
The Government can proceed with the offensive measure of closure on the Bill if the Opposition shows that it is serious. For that to happen, though, the Conservative Party would have to put up an equal number of speakers to those put up by this Party, and obviously it does not intend to. Occasionally it does put up a speaker to make a token representation. If Members of that caucus were to join our caucus in an equal commitment to stop legislation, then they would put up three speakers for every one from this Party, but since it has taken the opposite
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
approach, clearly it intends to let the Bill slide through. In the hour that remains, we are faced with the necessity of putting up six speakers from the New Democratic Party with little assistance from the Conservative Party. That is consistent with the position the Conservatives have taken on the amendment as well as on the Bill itself and on Bill C-124.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext: Nonsense!

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
A commitment by the Conservatives such as 1 have outlined, would force the Government to impose closure on the Bill, but obviously they do not intend to bring that about.
On the 16 votes that were held in relation to Bill C-124, essentially the Conservative Party backed the Government. There was a proposal that Bill C-124 should not apply to pensions, but by voting with the Government the Conservatives elected to defeat that. It is clear that you cannot have your cake and eat it. We are not attacking our Conservative colleagues. I think many of them and a minority of Liberals believe the Bill is offensive. All we are doing at this time is asking the Conservative caucus to bear its full share of responsibility in order to defeat this reprehensible piece of legislation.
I ask them not to talk out of both sides of their mouths, blatantly claiming that they are doing their share to defeat the Bill.
Much has been said about this amendment already, Mr. Speaker. We know that the proposal would cap the pensions of 119,670 retired civil servants, 31,811 retired members of the Canadian Armed Forces and 2,249 retired RCMP officers, and that with increases in the years ahead, roughly 200,000 people, including spouses, would be affected.
The Government is asking us to take the money that those people have paid into a pension plan and money paid to index that pension plan and use it to refuel the economic recovery of the country. Clearly that is a complete and reprehensible farce proposed by a reprehensible Government.
Over the years, the mismanagement of the economy, the blatant abuse of Canadians through high interest rates, the lack of development of an industrial strategy, the failure to provide adequate programs for industrial development and secondary industry, have led to the collapse of the economy. The way out of this is not to steal from retired civil servants or retired members of the Canadian Armed Forces but, rather, to put an adequate program of economic development in front of Parliament, pass it quickly and get Canada back on the road to economic recovery. I reiterate, the solution is not to steal from civil servants.
The amendment before us which proposes to give back a small amount of money, represents an attack by both the Liberals and the Conservatives on the concept of the Public Service. They know full well that if they spread the view that public servants are not doing a good job then, by implication, it follows that their pensions should be chopped, their bargaining rights taken away and their salaries capped. When the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) was a member of the

January 18, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2}
Clark Government he proposed to chop the civil service by 60,000 members.

speechtext: The Six-million-dollar man.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:

What we have before us today is a grossly unfair amendent which is a complete insult. It shows a lack of integrity on the part of the Government and a lack of commitment by the Conservative Party to retired civil servants, members of the Armed Forces and the RCMP.

subtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO MODIFY BENEFIT INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the opportunity to speak on this amendment and some of the general principles involved in the Bill. I should like to raise some issues of a moral and ethical nature. First, I should like to remind members of the Government about the Speech from the Throne of April 14, 1980.
We are now in one of the longest sessions of Parliament in history. Because of this, perhaps our Liberal friends opposite have forgotten what was said in that Speech from the Throne, so I think it is important to remind them. They made a commitment to the people in April 1980 which is not being honoured. The Government promised to respond to individual needs by promoting greater security for the elderly, extended opportunities for the young and equality for women. Does this Bill offer that greater security, Mr. Speaker? It definitely does not. My colleagues have pointed out that many of the older pensioners are women. In my constituency there are some who worked for the federal civil service in Ottawa and who took early retirement. Do you think they consider this to be equality? They definitely do not.
In that same Speech from the Throne in 1980, the Liberals claimed that they wanted to create a country whose people would share their wealth with those who need it most. But what is being done for the elderly and the pensioners of this country? The Government is attacking their pensions.
The Speech from the Throne pointed out that inflation strikes hardest at the old and those least able to take care of themselves, yet the Government is now acting in an irresponsible manner.
I notice that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is in her place. In committee she said that she expected sacrifices from everyone, from taxpayers in general,
Family Allowance recipients and pensioners. This reminds me of the little anecdote about the hen and the hog walking arm and arm and seeing a sign at a church concerning an offering. The hen said to the hog, "I have an idea. I think we should contribute to the needs of the poor; I think we should offer them bacon and eggs." The hog replied, "Well, yes, for you that is merely an offering, but for me it would be a total sacrifice." Many of these elderly people have already sacrificed totally. These people had to live through the more difficult periods of time when they did not have all the technology and other benefits we have today. They had to live by the sweat of their brow. These people are presently being attacked.
I should like to share the contents of one or two letters that I received because we need to remind the Government opposite that it is the human dimension it needs to take into consideration. In one letter from Ste. Rose du Lac in my riding, a person wrote:
I have worked for nearly 21 years in the Post Office-the first years were made up of long hours and days and very hard work-we were there to give service to our community.
The contributions made to the SRB Fund were mandatory and represented a form of insurance of our pensions against rising costs of living. We paid the premium. We are entitled to it.
Now a retired pensioner, I have looked forward to that pension cheque so I can enjoy the rest of my declining years.
She asked me to do everything possible to stop this type of legislation. In another letter from Winnipegosis in my riding, a superannuate referred to Bill C-133 and asked me to oppose it. It read:
This is in direct opposition to what we were promised when we contributed an extra 1 per cent which was to ensure that our pensions would be indexed according to the increase in the cost of living. We feel that we have paid the premium and so should be entitled to the insurance this premium was to cover.
If this Bill is passed it will give the Government the legal right to rob the pensioners of their rights and reduce many to living below the poverty level recently determined by the Senate. In other words it would reduce or rob the average pensioner of approximately $1,200 in the next two years and drastically lower their standard of living for years to come. The Government's claim that this lower indexation will save the pension account $100 million is a very misleading assertion. The $100 million belongs to the contributing public workers, not the Government.
On behalf of all superannuates and those now contributing to the fund, 1 would urge that you do everything in your power to oppose any legislation by our Government to alter the present form of indexation. I think you will realize that if this Bill is passed it will set a precedent which will endanger the rights of many people in Canada and also lead to possibly other legislation of a similar nature.
Again I would urge you to use all means you have available to have this Bill defeated.
I could go on and on sharing the comments of people who have taken the time to write to me. They have written in their own hand; it is not something they have cranked out. They are representative of the vital concerns of people who perhaps have been struck with fear as a result of the arrogant actions of the Government. Another letter reads:
I am writing to express my concern of Bill C-133 which is now before the House of Commons.
As I am a retired federal civil servant, I urge you and your colleagues to oppose this measure, in support of all retirees of the Civil Service.
January 18, 1983

I assure that person that indeed we oppose this Bill. Another letter urged me to strongly oppose the Bill to amend the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act.
There are some people who have waited for a long time to receive their pension. 1 have a letter from a person who retired as a warrant officer in 1971. He contributed to the pension fund and received a pension cheque of some $349, which amount had not changed since that date. However, a couple of years ago he received notification, according to his letter, that in 1983 his pension would be adjusted upward. He said that he was elated, but imagine his feelings when he found out that the Government would now renege on its commitment to indexation.
What is happening in this type of legislation? It is a case where the Government is failing to recognize the people who contributed over their earning years to the economy of Canada. The present Government is biting the hands that have fed it over the years. This type of ingratitude reflects negatively on the Government. I urge the Government to reconsider this legislation. In this case a contract was given to people; there was a promise and an understanding. Pensioners contributed with full trust and in confidence, expecting the Government to honour its word. Instead, the Government has not honoured its word.
Perhaps we should ask ourselves whether pensions are really a privilege or something actually earned by pensioners. I urge the Government to recognize that it is not a mere privilege. It is something to which people contributed, something for which public servants worked hard, something they have earned. Retired public servants in my community, even those who retired early, contribute in vital ways to community life, whether it be volunteer work, in cultural groups or otherwise. They anticipated that the Government would honour its word and that they would be able to cope with inflation because they had contributed to the fund. Some of them were enticed to take early retirement, feeling that this was one way in which they could assist in providing employment for younger people. Instead, the Government reneged on its promise and these people were forced to ask themselves whether they could get back into the job market to meet their needs in their retiring years.
In closing, I indicate to the Government that by its actions it is creating a crisis of confidence in itself. I urge Government members to have a change of heart, repent in their ways and drop this Bill.

I would like to have a little leeway before coming to the comments I would like to make with regard to the amendments to the Bill. One could hardly recognize what we are debating from listening to some of the interjections made by members of the Conservative Party. I am tired of listening to members of the Conservative Party blaming their woes and problems on the New Democratic Party, which Party they consider to have defeated the Conservative Government in December, 1979. Comments made this afternoon, both by the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) and the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) were almost entirely on that subject. I would like the people of Canada to know the reason for the downfall of the Conservative Government in December, 1979. The Government of the day, that Conservative Government, introduced a budget in which it set out to the people of Canada how the Conservatives would run the affairs of the country. The Liberals made an amendment to the budget. As normal procedure, the New Democratic Party made a sub-amendment to the amendment of the Liberals. When it came time to vote on the subamendment to the amendment, the subamendment which was put forth by the NDP, the Conservatives were defeated. They took that as a vote of non-confidence. In spite of requests and pleas from many members of the Progressive Conservative Party, their Leader went to the Governor General and asked for Parliament to be dissolved and to call another election. It was out of the ignorance of the Conservative Party, i submit that the Conservatives did not have to go to the Governor General and have another election called. They could have waited until the amendment moved by the Liberals came to a vote or until the actual vote was taken on the budget itself. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and I think the people of Canada should know, that it was through ignorance and the inability of the leadership in the Conservative Party that brought the Conservatives down in 1979. It was through no fault of the New Democratic Party that that Government was removed.
