I would like to address the rest of my remarks to the Bill itself and to the amendment. By the Government's own admission, it will save in 1983 some $60 million by imposing a

January 18, 1983
Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act (No. 2)
6.5 per cent limitation on the indexation of retired public employees' pensions. If the Government invested all of the $60 million that we will have at the end of this fiscal year, this $60 million in savings would make up one twenty-fifth of one per cent of the national debt. That is a very minuscule amount when you talk about the whole scheme of things. In 1984, the Government will be saved an additional $105 million.
My colleagues and I in the New Democratic Party are opposed to this amendment as we are opposed to Bill C-133 itself. We do not see any need to put the burden of fighting inflation or of beating inflation to the ground on the backs of those who can least afford it.
In the pension plan right now that we are talking about today, there are some 90,000 former contributors who receive about $8,100 annually out of the program. There are an additional 32,500 people who receive about $3,200 a year each in survivor's benefits. The average annual pension that was paid out, as of November, 1982, was some $6,900 a pensioner under this pension program.
I think it is unfair for the Government to have said there is not a contract here. I submit that there certainly is a contract, if not written or entrenched in stone, there was certainly an agreement between the public employees and the Government that they would be taken care of in their years of retirement as part of having worked and served their country and also as a benefit for having contributed 6.5 per cent of their salaries. This was to assure the public employees some kind of security in their retirement. In addition to this, these people have paid an extra one per cent of their income to protect their pensions against the ravages of inflation with which we have become so familiar in recent years. As the cost of living went up according to the Consumer Price Index, their pensions also would go up. It is important to note that these retired public employees paid for that benefit.
In the 1960s the Government suggested that superannuation be excluded from collective bargaining. In return, the public employees were promised that there would be no unilateral changes in the program. An advisory committee was established and, until the present time, the Government kept its promise, but now it is breaking the promise. This is the same as in the early days when the private pensions and public pension programs were not in existence. The railways were the most flagrant abusers of pension programs. The railways used a pension program as a tool to hang over the heads of their employees so they could clout them with it if they went on strike. When people went on strike their pension programs were cancelled. In that case, many people within the union were divided. The younger people, not caring quite as much for their pensions, would still want to go out and fight whereas those closest to retirement could not do that because they knew the companies could take away their pensions from them at any time.
We find the Government is doing much the same thing here in destroying confidence in the Canadian people. People felt they had a contract. They thought the Government was obligated in terms of providing them with some retirement income. But we now find the Government has been reneging
on the promise of protecting them from the ravages of inflation. In fact, it will be very harmful to this small group of people since we have, relatively speaking, a small dollar amount that will not even affect the treasuries of Canada. It is hard to say how actuarially sound the program is because the Government does not set up separate accounts for the indexing amount put in by public employees and the actual benefit that has to be covered for the 6.5 per cent. The moneys go into general revenues, and it is very difficult to trace back how sound the pension program is when the Government keeps the records for the pension program in the way that it does.
I will say a further word in terms of support of this Bill. One finds that when the six and five program first came about in Bill C-124, the Liberals introduced it and the Conservatives supported it, knowing full well that what was going to happen to this program is happening here today. The only Party on record as being opposed to the changes in the pension programs for which we have fought so long and hard is the New Democratic Party. It is certainly not the fault of our pensioners or our retired public employees that the country has suffered such a high rate of inflation. It is direction, or lack of it, from successive Governments, both Liberal and Conservative, which have not put this country on the track on which it should be.
We need to bolster our economy in order to protect those programs which we have worked so long and hard to put into place. While Governments are partly responsible for bringing this to reality, we now see it being eroded.
I am very distressed to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), who is returning from his tour, indicating that we may be shifting some of our exports of raw material to Japan since the United States is no longer as great an industrial power. I believe this is a sad situation. I suggest that we should be attempting to process some of those resources at home instead of exporting them to other countries, so that we may provide the jobs and the economy that we need in Canada and protect those programs which are being affected by Bill C-133 and C-131.

They ran on the horse of Reaganomics and those foreign ideologies about the new morality and the new conservative trend from south of the 49th parallel, and we are beginning to see the results of that.
I believe that these two old Parties want to reduce indexing and eventually have no indexing, in spite of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) believed a few years ago.
Every Canadian would be willing to co-operate in fighting inflation and providing employment. When the Government unfairly picks on those who are at the lower end of the income scale and unable to defend themselves, then this Party cannot and will not support that unfair treatment. We will do what we can to prevent this legislation from passing.
Even with a modest amount of inflation, or even zero inflation, the necessity for an increase in pension will still arise to allow for an increase in the standard of living. However, we will not likely reach that stage for some time.
1 would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the legislation with which we are confronted is reminiscent of former policies. I invite my friends on the Government side and in the Official Opposition to go back and read Hansard of 1929 and through the "Dirty Thirties". We are now into our 116th year of Confederation and we have had nothing but Grits and Tories and Tories and Grits, booms and busts, depressions and booms and recessions and busts. It is a vicious circle.
It is interesting to consider that this legislation attacks the pensions of former federal employees whose pensions were part of their wage package. Every government or private employer has taken into account the expenditures it has had to make for unemployment insurance premiums, workmen's compensation and its share of pension deductions as part of the wage package. Since it was considered as part of the wage package, private sector employers were able to add that to their cost of doing business. Working people considered deductions for a pension as part of the wages they earned in all the years they were employed. It is their money and not the Government's to make use of. That is money which the Government holds in trust for federal civil service pensioners.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak against Bill C-133, and particularly this amendment, which is an insult.
I agree with the concept of Government restraint. The record shows that we voted in favour of the restraint program of the federal Government. I would like to make it perfectly clear now that the vote was not also a vote in favour of breaking faith with the many public service pensioners who will be affected by Bill C-133. I find it very disturbing that, as part of the federal Government's so-called restraint program, it has decided to penalize public sector pensioners. 1 am deeply concerned that this Government, reversing its repeated promise for a just and equitable tax system, is now adopting a proposal which clearly discriminates against a segment of the population who are the most susceptible to the vagaries of this recession-wracked economy, elderly pensioners.
Indexation of our tax system affords taxpayers a measure of protection against inflation and at the same time imposes a degree of financial discipline and spending control of the federal Treasury. With this proposal, the Government will profit from inflation through the erosion of the income of civil service pensions. No incentive will exist for this Government to try to halt the inflation spiral. Unlike those Canadians who, despite Liberal policies, are working, pensioners are not able to negotiate increases to their incomes to help them cope with rising costs. That is why the fully indexed pension is so necessary. It enables men and women on fixed incomes to keep the purchasing power they have when they retire. The argument that the universal old age pension goes equally to the well-off as to the needy elderly, does not apply. The very needy elderly are eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement, which continues to be fully indexed. The well-off elderly are in a fortunate position. However, there are about 100,000 elderly recipients of universal old age pensions whose outside incomes are just barely above the $6,000 cut-off for the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
The Senate of Canada maintains that a two-person family earning less than $11,030 in 1980, a figure which must be higher now considering this Government's track record of recessionary policies, live in abject poverty. Former public sector workers and their survivors currently receive an average of only $6,900 per year. In large cities, pensioners live well below the poverty line. While $55 may not seem to be a large amount of money, to many pensioners who have planned for their retirement, next year this amount will be very important.

NATIONAL SECURITY-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT VIS-A-VIS SOVIET GOVERNMENT. (B) REQUEST FOR REDUCTION IN NUMBER OF SOVIET EMBASSY OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to address, at some greater length, a question which I asked of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on December 10, 1982, and the response to that question.
It will be recalled that my concern, expressed in Hansard at page 21474, involved the spy Hambleton and the revelation that in a British court, not a Canadian court, the country for whom Hambleton was engaged in his spying activities was the Soviet Union. Having regard to that disclosure, I asked the Prime Minister what note of protest his Government has sent to the dictatorial regime in the Kremlin. He confronted me with the response, which is on record, that to the best of his knowledge there has been no specific protests at that time.
I then went on to deal with the fundamental problem that exists with respect to the staffing of the Soviet embassy by agents of the KGB, either properly so-called or otherwise. I pointed out to the Prime Minister that this was not a novel or unusual circumstance in that it was not that long ago that 12 employees of the Soviet embassy had been expelled from Canada for conducting espionage activities. His response to me was that that showed very clearly that the Government was indeed on its toes, astute and alert and about to deal with those who tampered with our national security.
Let me refer to Hansard for April 2, 1982 when almost the exact circumstance was raised by myself in the House. I refer to page 16098. In that case I referred to the expulsion from Canada of a certain Mikhail Abramov, an official of the Soviet embassy who was carrying out activities which were illegal
January 18, 1983

under Canadian law. Accordingly, he was denied continued residence in this country. It will be recalled that Mr. Abramov had endeavoured, unsuccessfully that time, to convince a Canadian citizen to provide him with information of a technical nature which had been denied the Soviet Government as a consequence of its invasion of Afghanistan.
On that occasion I referred to a statement by the then secretary of state for External Affairs, now the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan), in which he dealt with the revelations of the espionage activities of Mr. Abramov. That particular press release noted that "this is the third time in a period of four years that Russians have been involved in activities of this nature." With the Hambleton affair, we might now conclude that there were four occurrences within a four-year period, or maybe three and a half-years. In any event, the circumstance with which we are confronted is one in which the Soviet Union consistently breaches our laws and engages in activities which are directly related to efforts made by their agents to subvert Canadian justice and penetrate our security.
The point I made in both cases was simply this. It is time we laid down a rule to the Soviet Union that they would understand. I suggested that that rule be this. In the event that an agent of the Soviet Union is found to be engaging in subversive acts in Canada or endeavouring to tamper with our security system or enticing Canadians to commit treason, for every expelled Soviet diplomat or agent, five of their embassy staff shall be expelled. This would be done in the hope and expectation that by reducing the number of these agents, the security of Canada may be protected.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: NATIONAL SECURITY-POSITION OF CANADIAN GOVERNMENT VIS-A-VIS SOVIET GOVERNMENT. (B) REQUEST FOR REDUCTION IN NUMBER OF SOVIET EMBASSY OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his comment to the effect that, in his view, the Government is alert and on its toes, ready to protect our national security. I believe those were his exact words and he is correct in that analysis.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) replied to this question on December 10 he said that the Government does not hesitate to demand the withdrawal of personnel from Canada who have abused their diplomatic status or who have behaved in ways contrary to their responsibilities as representatives of their countries. This includes the Soviet Union. The record shows that Canada has been prepared to take appropriate action as circumstances dictate. Indeed, since 1978, a total of 18 foreign officials from four different countries have been declared persona non grata. The Hon. Member should know that prompt and firm action is certainly taken against all foreign officials who abuse their diplomatic status.
It is important, however, to repeat that diplomats are posted to Canada for valid and entirely legitimate reasons. They have important functions to fulfill representing their countries' interests here, just as our representatives have in their countries. We encourage normal diplomatic functions by any
Adjournment Debate
embassy and we expect that same treatment for our representatives abroad.
In the case of the Soviet Union, we are aware that in the past some officials have abused their status and we have reacted appropriately. A permanent reduction in the number of Soviet Embassy staff, however, would certainly not guarantee that such unacceptable activities would end. It would, however, undoubtedly invite retaliation against our Embassy in Moscow and inevitably it would adversely affect the important work carried out by both embassies in managing Canada-Soviet relations. If we applied the Hon. Member's magical rule of five expulsions for every sin, then we would expect the same treatment to be meted out to our people in Moscow. That would not be useful.

UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-PLIGHT OF PERSONS EXHAUSTING BENEFITS-REQUEST FOR AID TO MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this evening I would like to raise a very special problem which has occurred in certain parts of Canada, namely, the two communities of Kamloops and Salmon Arm, British Columbia.
The unemployment rate in Kamloops as of last week was 27.4 per cent, and in Salmon Arm it was in excess of 30 per cent. These communities have had to adjust to an extremely trying situation and they have done so by formulating a series of food bank operations for needy families. They have set up unemployment guidance centres to advise on both economic and social aspects which face a family or individual experiencing unemployment, particularly those who have been unemployed for more than a year and who are now part of that growing group called "exhausties" who have lost their UIC benefits and are now dependent upon welfare or other forms of social assistance. The mayors of the communities have established special employment crisis centres. Local groups are again doing a variety of volunteer tasks to ease the unemployment problem which now face so many families in these two communities.
The question, Mr. Speaker, is this. What does the Federal Government have for these communities faced with these very special problems at this time? We hear of programs such as ILAP, under which a certain community is designated because of a high level of unemployment and the difficult circumstances it faces. I should like to ask how much unemployment is required before a community is designated under that scheme to provide financial assistance to both the public and private sector. It seems to me that 27 per cent and 30 per cent unemployment is far in excess of the statistics for those communities that have already received designations under programs such as ILAP.
I should like to ask the Government to consider these two communities as being in some special circumstances, and give special consideration to them for public works projects, for instance, that could be financed through a number of federal Government schemes.

The fundamental question my constituents have asked me to pose to the Government is, how many people have to be unemployment before a community is considered eligible for special assistance from the federal Government?
It has been proposed that the period for which people receive UI benefits should be extended in special circumstances. At the present time, many people who have received benefits for 52 weeks no longer qualify and see their incomes collapse to the social welfare level. Some of them end up losing their homes, their businesses, their farms or whatever.
I realize that people sometimes describe situations in terms that make them seem worse than they are, but 27 per cent and 30 per cent unemployment in a community means that the situation is very severe indeed. It does not look as if things will get much better in the months ahead. Like everyone else, I hope that economic recovery is just around the corner, but until we see some clear evidence of it 1 suspect that unemployment will increase.
I ask the Member of the Government who will reply, and for whom I have a great deal of respect, to give these two hard-pressed communities some encouragement so that they may approach the future with optimism.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I immediately tell the Hon. Member that he has raised his concerns at a most appropriate time, just before the presentation of a budget by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). I am certain that these representations, among others, will be considered seriously by the Minister in the preparation of that document.
I think we should offer a small explanation on each of the two issues he has raised. He asked about a universal increase in the benefit period for unemployment insurance and also about increasing some tax rates in order to pay for that. In good conscience, he discussed the communities where unemployment is running at 30 and 40 per cent. His proposal to increase benefits would also apply, however, in an area like my own where we are fortunate enough to have an 8 per cent unemployment rate. I think we need to target the help more to distressed communities rather than making it universal. In an area like mine, unemployed people have communities like Toronto, Mississauga, Oakville, Burlington and Guelph in which to approach employers in thousands of businesses for work. Those people would benefit as much as those people in isolated places. For that reason we introduced targeted programs like ILAP and NEED.
I would refer the Hon. Member specifically to the municipal options available under the NEED program through which communities can build up their infrastructure and, at the same time, hire people who are exhausting their benefits. In that way, they can kill two birds with the one stone. They can get rid of some of the headaches that up to now the municipalities have not been able to solve.
The tax question is equally important and equally serious. I urge the Hon. Member to look at the advantages of leaving the money in the private sector where it can stimulate investment
and where it can stimulate the creation of jobs. In effect, we have already had a tax increase, the increase in unemployment insurance premiums in October to both employers and employees.
I do not think it would be appropriate to drain more money out of the private sector at this time just to increase the period of time for universal unemployment insurance benefits. We should be looking at targeted programs and we should be encouraging investment. At the same time I encourage the Hon. Member to continue making his representations so that the Minister can take them into account in the preparation of his next budget.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-LEVEL OF BEEF IMPORTS. (B) BALANCE REMAINING IN QUOTAS
AGRICULTURE-LEVEL OF BEEF IMPORTS. (B) BALANCE REMAINING IN QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my adjournment debate participation this evening is related to questions I directed to the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) respecting the matter of recent beef imports into Canada. The details can be found in Hansard of November 5, as reported on pages 20447 and 20448.
At that time I asked whether current beef imports into Canada were being properly monitored according to an earlier September meeting between the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and some of his staff and the newly-appointed Meat Import Advisory Committee. This monitoring procedure was necessary because of the then anticipated reduction in Canadian exports of beef to the United States under the terms of the U.S. meat import law.
This year-end disruption of beef imports and exports between Canada and the United States was precipitated by the ongoing very serious drought in Australia. This situation, which was really tragic in that country, interrupted the last half of their 1982 exports into North America and caused considerable disruption. It caused stepped-up beef exports from Australia to both the United States and Canada, but mainly into the United States because its market was obviously higher.
In his response the Minister admitted to the danger of "some of that excess being diverted into Canadian markets". Now we have a better understanding of what developed after Australia, New Zealand and Canada voluntarily agreed to reduce and limit their beef exports to the United States, in return, for which the United States would not trigger its reduced beef import law quotas to which they were entitled. Unfortunately it took Canadian authorities more than a month to put this quota control into effect.
In October 1982 the Government announced that Canada's quota had been filled, and we began to experience a serious drop in our Canadian live cow prices. Our shipment of live cows had been increasing since the United States beef quota had been applied. Two situations developed. Our live cow prices were depressed rather significantly and the incident
January 18, 1983

provided a short-term but serious irritant to American cattlemen. I know from my own experience that something like this upsets a usually good relationship between our two countries. This was all because of the delay of over a month in the Canadian Government's institution of the export permit system to provide a basis of monitoring.
The voluntary import limitation agreement was the right approach; I hasten to point that out. It was fully supported and suggested in the first place by the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. The Association also suggested quarterly quotas for the new year that we are into now. Unfortunately the joint statement at the end of last year, on December 30, did not suggest this. The reason is obvious.
We know the threat of excessive imports exceeding quotas at this time is not very likely. Nevertheless, this experience in 1982 suggests that not only should a quota have been declared in that joint statement at the end of last year by the Minister of State for International Trade and the Minister of Agriculture. But also, we feel sure, and the Canadian Cattlemen's Association recommended, that it be should done on a quarterly basis.
I would suggest one other recommendation I hope the Government will take seriously. When we have an upsetting situation or an emergency, such as took place in the last six or seven weeks of 1982, which requires a voluntary quota system, such as we used, a monitoring permit system should be declared early, giving the trade-not only the producers but the importers and exporters-to get used to the fact that they can expect a monitoring system under the Export and Import Permits Act.
This should be done early enough so that we do not have the panic effect we had last fall. Even though the Government indicated what it would do, it took a long time to implement the monitoring process. That had rather serious consequences on the price of our live cattle, in particular.
There is one other point concerning this situation that 1 think is worth mentioning. Surely this is the time to think about the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. We had one preliminary early meeting late last fall. This reminds us of the situation that developed in the discussions that took place in the Tokyo round during the last GATT negotiations a little over three years ago. Now that is behind us and we see the situation that developed. We know our negotiators were outmanoeuvred in the Tokyo round in two areas.
The first was the guaranteed minimum access level, to which Canada subscribed, for meat imports coming into Canada, mostly from Australia, New Zealand and the United States. It was set too high. I think that is obvious now. Perhaps the reason is that at the time of the negotiations Canada had an all-time high in our cattle population. That situation has drastically changed. It may be years before we ever reach that peak again. But let us remember, such is not the time to
Adjournment Debate
negotiate a guaranteed minimum access level. The figure set has caused us considerable trouble.
The second thing that developed out of those negotiations was our agreement as a trading partner to what is known as a human population growth factor. No other country, especially the United States, was asked to make such an agreement. This was an agreement that as our human population increased each year, which is inevitable, so should the level of imports of Canada. That has imposed a long-term load on what we are expected to take into Canada. This is very discouraging to our domestic cattle producers at a time when they need some incentive to get back into the industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance);
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-LEVEL OF BEEF IMPORTS. (B) BALANCE REMAINING IN QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the points raised by the Hon. Member. I will make sure they are drawn to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan).
The Hon. Member pointed out the events of 1982. I would like to note further that on September 28, the Governments of Canada and the United States entered into an arrangement to control the trade in beef and veal for the calendar year ending December 31, 1982. The two Governments anticipated that Canadian exports of beef and veal to the United States would not exceed 121.1 million pounds and that U.S. exports of beef and veal to Canada would not exceed 21.4 million pounds, both figures for 1982.
Consequently, beef and veal were placed on the Export Control List and the Import Control List effective October 1, thereby requiring export and import permits for the last quarter of 1982.
On December 31, 1982, the Minister of State for International Trade and the Minister of Agriculture announced that upon review of the international meat situation, Canadian import controls would not be required for at least the initial 1983 period. In addition, a review of the U.S. beef market indicated that, at least for the first two-quarters of 1983, it would not be necessary to restrict beef exports to the U.S. In view of these developments, the requirements for export and import permits were revoked, effective January 1, 1983.
The Minister of agriculture has added, however, that the decision not to limit imports of beef and veal in 1983 would be reviewed on a quarterly basis-and that is close to what was said in one of the comments by the Hon. Member-and that import action would be considered if the forecast for imports of beef and veal increased significantly, or if the United States moved to restrict its own beef and veal imports.
